title: Sacral Sound, Unbearable Noise, and Cairene Masculinities
abstract: The epigraph explains how the call to prayer functions as a sonic reminder of a sacral community. In this article I explore how sound is also connected to activists’ masculinities and space where the soundscape of the adhan in Cairo transforms from desired sacral sound to unwanted noise atmospheres (see Eisenlohr 2018). The aim is also to understand the “subjective, ‘political’ attribute of noise” in relation to gender and belonging (Pickering and Rice 2017: 1). Focusing on sound or noise in relation to gender makes it possible to see how “sensory knowledge develops through ongoing interaction with the environment” (Rice 2010: S43). Listening can create community or dissolve it. Understanding gender through the prism of sound unfolds the tensions among (and ongoing creation of) specific gendered subjects in relation to state power, communities, and space.In Cairo, political unrest and its repression over the past decade (indeed, in the past few years, there has not been space for actual political unrest) has produced new imaginaries and maps of unbelonging for political dissidents, who are deprived of the freedom of expression and the right to safety and access to particular spaces, such as, for instance, by the closure of the cafés in el-Bustan in Downtown Cairo. Sound and acts of listening position humans in space but also create gendered selves and public empathy through an amalgam of aesthetics and sensibility.The autocratic military regime in Egypt, in power since the 2013 coup, has consciously disciplined and molded its citizens by, among other things, forbidding particular religious sounds while repeating the sound of the national anthem on the radio and using unbearably loud sounds during torture (Winegar 2014). Religious sounds in Egypt are not neatly associated with the state but with what Charles Hirschkind (2006) calls an Islamic counterpublic, which makes them affectively just as loaded for Cairene atheist intellectuals as are military soundscapes. The nation is modeled after the family, as Rim Naguib (2020: 51) has stated, in which “the nation and the masculine qualities of the military leader are contrasted with the femininity of a dependent nation, imagined as the passive object of the masculine patriotic act of salvation and protection. Patriarchal binaries are projected onto the relation between state and nation, military and civilian, thereby demobilizing and subordinating the people to autocratic military rule.” Since the ousting of President Mohamed Morsi during the summer of 2013, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s autocratic military regime has created a sense of belonging among some Egyptians while producing a widespread sense of alienation, through which both Muslim Brotherhood supporters and liberal activists are constructed as enemies and terrorists and suspected of a lack of loyalty to the nation (Malmström 2019).For me, it is key to explore the production of masculinities as an open-ended life process, actively shaped by both agency and victimhood, and to affirm the role of embodiment (Malmström 2015). I am inspired by one scholar in particular, Andrija Filipović (2017), in the field of sound, space, and the making of straight and queer masculinities. Filipović examines how straight masculinity and queer subjectivities are made in affective relation to the sounds within various spaces, challenging the “boundaries” between the private and public in the urban soundscape of Belgrade.Furthermore, soundscapes that one person finds tranquil may strike another as sinister; noise can feel liberating for one and oppressive for another. Noise is a concept that has many definitions; David Novak (2015: 125) writes about noise as a context of sensory experience but also as “a moving subject of circulation, of sound and listening, that emerges in the process of navigating the world and its differences.” Andrija Filipović (2018: 215–16) writes that the noise of urban soundscapes can be “a phenomenon that consists of both signifying and nonsignifying layers, which act on and are acted upon by the multiplicity of the bodies moving through the urban landscape.” Hugh Pickering and Tom Rice (2017) state that many sound scholars have described noise as “sound out of place,” drawing on Mary Douglas’s classic definition of dirt as “matter out of place.” My argument in the context of noise is that to understand the way sound is involved in social processes, one must acknowledge that “noise is mainly a subjective classification” (Pickering and Rice 2017). Noise can be an unintended by-product of a technological environment, but it can also be a conscious sonic violence intended to disorient or disable people (Goodman 2012; Malmström 2014).Mosques actively participate in the production of Cairo’s vibrant soundscape with five calls to prayer, day and night. But what happens when the sonic infrastructures of one of the institutions of the state daily penetrate the porous borders of home, when, at the same time, political activists are threatened by the power of the same state’s sound infrastructure? The institutions of state power (including the Ministry of Endowments) in Egypt employ sound as a political representation as well as monitor and threaten through the sonic. A law to unify the call to prayer was issued in 2010 but was halted after the January 25 revolution in 2011. The sound of the state reminds the activists of the failure of their fierce struggle for “bread, freedom and social justice” (ʿaysh, hurriyya, ʿadala igtimaʿiyya) in 2011. The current regime has no intention of catering to any of them, instead focusing on megaprojects such as the building of the new capital, to which they are moving all government ministries and the presidential complex (Michaelson 2018) and the new Suez Canal tunnels (Ahram Online 2018), in addition to the focus on surveillance and the war on terror. As we know, there are always conflicting demands that need to be satisfied in people’s lives, and the life journey of activists, whether atheists or not, is never static. We should therefore expect ambivalence. People are constantly living through ambivalence, contradictions, and experiences of failure, as Samuli Schielke (2015) highlights in his ethnography of the before, during, and after of the 2011 political revolts in Egypt.The Cairene men in focus in this article refer to themselves as muthaqqafin, or intellectuals. They attend local coffee shops and bars in Downtown Cairo almost every evening on weekdays and nightclubs on weekends (fig. 1). Today they talk explicitly about palpable responses (their own and those of others) of affective politics, such as suspicion, depression, denial, anger, fatigue, and a sense of hopelessness that developed after the summer of 2013.The fieldwork for this project was carried out in Cairo from September 2013 to the end of January 2018 as well as during the fall of 2019. All names have been changed in light of the politically sensitive nature of the subject matter, and all other information about the interlocutors is omitted to protect their safety. I have conducted fieldwork in Egypt since 2001. All these years of lived experiences, as a woman (from young to middle age) with a “halfie” background (Scandinavian and Middle Eastern) operating under different rules, have helped me build broad networks and trust and given me access to both male and female spaces (see Winegar 2012).I employ collaboration as a research tool. The men shared their lived experiences, and we shared experiences together. I have moved with collaborators through, in, and around the cityscape as they drove, walked, traveled, and socialized. I followed how events, actions, and interpretations unfolded as a way to gain an understanding of the fluid and ambiguous material reality that people experience. I observed how men performed, protested, and claimed belonging through their body language and voices in coffee shops and bars, where I paid attention to how and to what extent the men participated in political conversations as well as how they made claims of power and status or the lack thereof.My two interlocutors, Mohamad and Ali, belong to the same political crowd of Downtown Cairenes. I met them through mutual Cairene friends, although they cannot be described as close friends. These men are Egyptian citizens who, following the current paranoid military dictatorship’s tactics to control its oppositional citizens via total repression of political bodies, have effectively been deemed enemies of the state. I selected these two accounts to show how Mohamad and Ali have different perceptions of the adhan, although both are ambivalent in their responses. At the same time, they oppose both the autocratic state and the Muslim Brotherhood.Ali is a professional musician and activist whom I met through common friends in the fall of 2017. Ali was careful to praise the food before he ate, and he thanked God after every meal. However, Ali did not pray. His dark green prayer rug hung unused over a cupboard in his bedroom, like a reminder artifact of piety. I perceived Ali as very stressed, not least because of his lack of money. He struggled every day to find gigs or day jobs to afford the basics, like food and hygiene products, and every month he had to ask his landlord for a grace period to pay the rent. Ali had called on the generosity of others too many times. People around him were tired of lending money they scarcely had for fear of not getting it back. Ali repeatedly told me that he would start to pray again once he had found balance in life. I observed that he smoked and drank a lot of hashish and alcohol, probably to cope.Music was everything for Ali. He not only performed music but listened to different genres such as reggae, jazz, or blues every day and every hour. The only rupture of these loud sounds was when the muezzin performed the call to prayer. Immediately he turned off his computer and silenced others’ profane sounds, including conversations if friends were around, and praised God explicitly. I noticed that Ali’s body movements changed as well, altering into stillness. Another changed behavior I noticed, when I was in his house during one muezzin call, was that he immediately stopped kissing his girlfriend. When I asked him why, he explained that it was forbidden to kiss during the sacred sounds of prayer.I noticed, however, that Ali experienced the sacred sounds in a conflicting way. He told me that one reason was the bad quality of many of the speakers in the cityscape and that the speakers were not synchronized. A third reason was the voices of the muezzins themselves, as their oral sacral messages were often unmusical in combination with a loud volume. As a believing Muslim, Ali seemed to experience the calls as sacral sounds, but as a talented musician, he lived through these sounds as noises. I noticed that his body language became stressed when listening to too many dissonances. It was as if he struggled and reluctantly resisted the sonic environment. It seemed as though Ali listened to sacrosanct sounds just as he listened to noise. He underscored that only muezzins with musical voices should be hired and told me once that his wish, if he had money, would be to buy excellent-quality speakers and synchronize them throughout Egypt. If we listen to Ali, we can follow how audible dissonance produced by shoddy loudspeakers, calls from multiple minarets, and the quality of the muezzin’s sonic expressions provokes irritation and intolerance, but simultaneously inhibits the listening subject as the adhan brings on a sense of the sacred. The aesthetics link up with technological transformations, which are also related to the ongoing tension of being the male subject Ali is striving to be. The noise is difficult to listen to, but it is also a daily reminder that he is not living the life a Muslim man is expected to live (failing to be a breadwinner and not praying, as well as using alcohol and drugs; see Ghannam 2013).I met Mohamad through political activist friends in 2014. Mohamad frequently attends local coffee shops and alternative bars for politically heated debates in Downtown Cairo. He sees himself as politically active, to the left, and defines himself as a secular Marxist and an intellectual. His family does not live in Cairo, and I have never met them, but Mohamad described them as strict, believing Muslims, orthodox in general, and upper middle class. I would say that through his background and upbringing, Mohamad is deeply influenced by Islam, something that is observable in his daily responses and actions. Nevertheless, it seemed as if it was very important for Mohamad to resist religion.I remember one occasion especially when the state forcefully infiltrated his body through sound. Mohamad and others were at a mutual friend’s home after a long Thursday night of bar hopping, which had ended with a stop at a popular nightclub. In the early dawn, when the muezzin called for the Friday morning prayer, Mohamad burst into a rage, shouting, “Kuss ummak” (Your mother’s cunt), as an immediate response. Mohamad listened to the sound of the muezzin as pure noise—for him, it was a noise of state violence. Maybe it was also a reminder of his past that stood in sharp contrast to his desire to make himself into the man he wanted to be.Although Mohamad always participated in intense, animated political discussions and gesticulated to underscore his standpoints—to show his status and manhood in the Downtown intellectual crowd—he was still too young and inexperienced (for example, he had not yet been detained, which was remarkable considering both his political actions and the crowd he hung out with) to be considered politically brave enough and the “manly man” he aspired to be in that milieu.Sherine Hafez (2012: 39) points out that “what the events of this uprising [2011] have revealed is that notions of masculinity undermined by a repressive regime have observably shifted the terms of the patriarchal bargain between genders and ages and between the state and its people.” The state demolishes the ability of these men to make a home, since the sonic vibrations penetrate the home’s porous walls and thereby destroy any borders between the outside and the inside. Through sound, the military state constantly reminds political activists that there is no space for alternative masculinities and no home for them in Egypt. As Filipović (2018: 214) states, when the sonic is incorporated into the analysis, the separation between the public and the private becomes contested.Farha Ghannam’s (2013) findings in Egypt reveal “the parallels people made between a proper government and a proper man: protection, support, and provision” (see, e.g., Amar 2013; Inhorn 2012; Kreil 2016; Rommel 2017; Schielke 2015). These ethnographic accounts show how sacral sounds transform into noise and how noise turns into sacral sounds. Mohamad’s and Ali’s experiences both expose immediate and embodied, albeit ambivalent, responses to the call to prayer. The sonic permeates the bodies of all men, but these urban sonic experiences are experienced differently, depending on individual and collective political bodies in relation to earlier lived experiences. In this article we can follow the ambivalent struggles and tensions of being a “proper man” in relation to both dominant gender discourses and alternative manhood. Much more research is needed to fully understand dictatorship in relation to what I tentatively define as unwanted masculinities, meaning all alternative masculinities opposing the current autocratic military regime (constructed as enemies and terrorists and suspected of a lack of loyalty to the nation) through the prism of sound.

title: Wagner on the Midway: Reassessing Sonic Divisions at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition
abstract: Among the millions of visitors who entered the gates of Chicago's 1893 World's Columbian Exposition was New York-based composer and folklorist Henry F. Gilbert. Like most other attendees, Gilbert was awed by the neoclassical architecture and the formal scientific, educational, and artistic displays in the section of the World's Columbian Exposition known as the White City. But he paid little attention to the performances in the White City's formal concert halls, instead homing in on the other half of the Exposition, the Midway Plaisance. Jutting perpendicularly away from the White City, the Midway was a moneymaking, quasi-anthropological venue with international exhibits. Entranced by what he called the “numerous and diverse twinges,” Gilbert attempted brief transcriptions of performances by the Midway's Algerian, Bedouin, Javanese, and Turkish musicians. But more unusually, he also noted the presence of music unexpected for our modern understanding of the Midway: selections from Richard Wagner's Lohengrin.1The appearance of Lohengrin on the Midway flies in the face of past interpretations of the 1893 World's Fair. Histories of the Exposition have told the story of two sonic opposites, the Midway and the White City, mirroring their physical and intentional division. The latter was dedicated to showcasing the greatest advances of Western nations while the Midway, scholars have argued, was mere entertainment, concerned with economics over edification and with offering commercialized culture to mass audiences. Within this duality, musicologists have approached the White City solely as a site for sacralized presentations of Euro-American music and the Midway, if studied at all, as an inauthentic site for folk musics. My analysis reveals that the World's Columbian Exposition had a largely undifferentiated soundscape where visitors experienced repertoire performed by a variety of ensembles in a multiplicity of contexts.2Previous research has only occasionally connected music with the World's Columbian Exposition (hereafter Exposition, World's Fair, or Fair) itself and stressed a rigid bifurcation between the Fair's two halves.3 James Gilbert's Perfect Cities, Lawrence Levine's Highbrow/Lowbrow, and Alan Trachtenberg's The Incorporation of America have been influential in cementing this view.4 Most musicologists have ignored the Midway, looking almost uniformly to the Fair's performance groups and ceremonies in the White City.5 This approach has cemented a narrow comprehension of musical activity at the Fair, favoring the Eurocentric narratives and history presented by the Exposition's leadership.Henry Gilbert's hearing of Lohengrin was not alone in challenging this view. Journalists, other visitors, guidebooks, and novels all positioned art music on the Midway, while Midway musicians occasionally performed non-Western music in the White City's prestigious concert halls, demonstrating blurred musical boundaries across the Fair despite the geographical and ideological divide. The same repertoire featured at formal orchestral concerts showcasing the presumed educational ethos of the White City was used more frequently for commercial and entertainment purposes. The Fair's porous soundscape demonstrates a popular culture shaped not only by Tin Pan Alley songs, patriotic marches, and appropriative tendencies, but also by Austro-German operatic and symphonic selections. There was not yet a firm divide between art and popular music.Held to honor the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus's landfall in the Western Hemisphere, the Exposition ran from May to October 1893. It proved an enormous success, as the more than 25 million visitors contributed to an overall budget surplus. With newspaper and magazine reports, the Fair's own The Daily Columbian, and a sizeable number of fictional and nonfictional accounts, the Exposition's influence spread far beyond the Midwest. It established Chicago as a rival to older cities on the Atlantic seaboard and cemented the United States as a global economic, industrial, and cultural force.The Fair's leadership, particularly President Harlow N. Higinbotham, directed an immense bureaucracy. The Department of Music was led by conductor Theodore Thomas, also the head of the official Exposition Orchestra, a 114-member ensemble, while Choral Director William Tomlins conducted the Exposition Chorus's 500 singers.6 Thomas was known throughout the country as a strong-willed conductor. Since the beginning of his career, Thomas had been one of the first conductors to change the nature of encores, which had previously been “unscheduled and complete repetitions of works” inserted throughout the program, preferring instead to restrict them (if encores were to occur at all) to the very end of the concert and limiting their length.7 Thomas introduced reserved seating in his concert halls and insisted upon uniform bowing by his string players.Thomas's notorious rigidity, though, soon ran afoul of the Exposition's Board of Directors. Thomas invited Ignacy Jan Paderewski to perform with the Exposition Orchestra in its first concert, for which Paderewski brought his own Steinway, setting off a chain of events described in the press as the “Great Piano War.” The Bureau of Music required musicians at the Exposition to use instruments made only by companies officially exhibiting at the Fair. Steinway & Sons chose not to display at the Fair, having no interest in being placed on the same level as dozens of other, smaller companies.8 After Paderewski's Steinway was smuggled into the Exposition under the darkness of night and used at both concerts, Thomas hung on to power for three months, leading performances as scheduled before he finally resigned; the official reason was economic.9 Max Bendix, the Exposition Orchestra's concertmaster, took the reins as de facto head of orchestral music, giving concerts with a smaller, re-formed Exposition Orchestra. In early September, when that project also failed, Bendix managed to gather a shifting group of musicians together, usually as a string quartet or piano quintet, to play smaller concerts until the final day of the Fair. Meanwhile, myriad band concerts, song recitals, instrumental programs, and near-daily organ performances—given by over a dozen organists—filled the gap left by the absence of Thomas and the full Exposition Orchestra.Higinbotham was also essential in driving the completion of the White City's masterplan, created by Daniel Burnham and a team of architects. While earlier designs entailed a range of modern styles, Burnham included only neoclassical, stucco-clad buildings in his “City Beautiful” approach. As visitors arrived in the Exposition's large railway station, they were met by the domed Administration Building with the central Court of Honor behind, replete with fountains and statuary. The main exhibition buildings radiated outwards, including the massive Manufactures and Liberal Arts Building, connected by Frederick Law Olmsted's curated landscapes. Many viewers observed the “dreamlike” quality of the Court of Honor, among them journalist Teresa Dean, who compared its appearance with tales from the “Arabian Nights” and described the buildings as “gleaming, sparkling, sunlit.”10 A sense of calm and majesty pervaded (in many visitor's reminiscences, at least), which suggested elegance and sophistication.11 Beyond a Venetian lagoon, with rose gardens on its enclosed Wooded Isle, government and state buildings dotted the landscape. Sites of less distinction in Burnham's mind, such as the Stock Pavilion, Dairy Buildings, and Anthropology Building, were situated on the edge of the White City.At the start of the Fair, Thomas's Bureau of Music provided funds for the creation of two concert halls: Music Hall and Festival (or Choral) Hall. These were large buildings, decorated with busts and statues of European composers, architecturally similar to the rest of Burnham's White City.12 One guidebook writes that Music Hall, the smaller of the two buildings, “impresses even the traveled beholder with its vastness.”13 It was in these two buildings that the grandest of ensembles performed, including the Exposition Orchestra, as well as the Columbian Chorus, Chicago Apollo Club, and visiting ensembles. While Festival Hall was closer to the Midway, befitting its role as a site of large-scale spectacles and ceremonies, Music Hall was far from the madding crowd, tucked on the lakefront just off the Court of Honor. title: Sacral Sound, Unbearable Noise, and Cairene Masculinities
abstract: The epigraph explains how the call to prayer functions as a sonic reminder of a sacral community. In this article I explore how sound is also connected to activists’ masculinities and space where the soundscape of the adhan in Cairo transforms from desired sacral sound to unwanted noise atmospheres (see Eisenlohr 2018). The aim is also to understand the “subjective, ‘political’ attribute of noise” in relation to gender and belonging (Pickering and Rice 2017: 1). Focusing on sound or noise in relation to gender makes it possible to see how “sensory knowledge develops through ongoing interaction with the environment” (Rice 2010: S43). Listening can create community or dissolve it. Understanding gender through the prism of sound unfolds the tensions among (and ongoing creation of) specific gendered subjects in relation to state power, communities, and space.In Cairo, political unrest and its repression over the past decade (indeed, in the past few years, there has not been space for actual political unrest) has produced new imaginaries and maps of unbelonging for political dissidents, who are deprived of the freedom of expression and the right to safety and access to particular spaces, such as, for instance, by the closure of the cafés in el-Bustan in Downtown Cairo. Sound and acts of listening position humans in space but also create gendered selves and public empathy through an amalgam of aesthetics and sensibility.The autocratic military regime in Egypt, in power since the 2013 coup, has consciously disciplined and molded its citizens by, among other things, forbidding particular religious sounds while repeating the sound of the national anthem on the radio and using unbearably loud sounds during torture (Winegar 2014). Religious sounds in Egypt are not neatly associated with the state but with what Charles Hirschkind (2006) calls an Islamic counterpublic, which makes them affectively just as loaded for Cairene atheist intellectuals as are military soundscapes. The nation is modeled after the family, as Rim Naguib (2020: 51) has stated, in which “the nation and the masculine qualities of the military leader are contrasted with the femininity of a dependent nation, imagined as the passive object of the masculine patriotic act of salvation and protection. Patriarchal binaries are projected onto the relation between state and nation, military and civilian, thereby demobilizing and subordinating the people to autocratic military rule.” Since the ousting of President Mohamed Morsi during the summer of 2013, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s autocratic military regime has created a sense of belonging among some Egyptians while producing a widespread sense of alienation, through which both Muslim Brotherhood supporters and liberal activists are constructed as enemies and terrorists and suspected of a lack of loyalty to the nation (Malmström 2019).For me, it is key to explore the production of masculinities as an open-ended life process, actively shaped by both agency and victimhood, and to affirm the role of embodiment (Malmström 2015). I am inspired by one scholar in particular, Andrija Filipović (2017), in the field of sound, space, and the making of straight and queer masculinities. Filipović examines how straight masculinity and queer subjectivities are made in affective relation to the sounds within various spaces, challenging the “boundaries” between the private and public in the urban soundscape of Belgrade.Furthermore, soundscapes that one person finds tranquil may strike another as sinister; noise can feel liberating for one and oppressive for another. Noise is a concept that has many definitions; David Novak (2015: 125) writes about noise as a context of sensory experience but also as “a moving subject of circulation, of sound and listening, that emerges in the process of navigating the world and its differences.” Andrija Filipović (2018: 215–16) writes that the noise of urban soundscapes can be “a phenomenon that consists of both signifying and nonsignifying layers, which act on and are acted upon by the multiplicity of the bodies moving through the urban landscape.” Hugh Pickering and Tom Rice (2017) state that many sound scholars have described noise as “sound out of place,” drawing on Mary Douglas’s classic definition of dirt as “matter out of place.” My argument in the context of noise is that to understand the way sound is involved in social processes, one must acknowledge that “noise is mainly a subjective classification” (Pickering and Rice 2017). Noise can be an unintended by-product of a technological environment, but it can also be a conscious sonic violence intended to disorient or disable people (Goodman 2012; Malmström 2014).Mosques actively participate in the production of Cairo’s vibrant soundscape with five calls to prayer, day and night. But what happens when the sonic infrastructures of one of the institutions of the state daily penetrate the porous borders of home, when, at the same time, political activists are threatened by the power of the same state’s sound infrastructure? The institutions of state power (including the Ministry of Endowments) in Egypt employ sound as a political representation as well as monitor and threaten through the sonic. A law to unify the call to prayer was issued in 2010 but was halted after the January 25 revolution in 2011. The sound of the state reminds the activists of the failure of their fierce struggle for “bread, freedom and social justice” (ʿaysh, hurriyya, ʿadala igtimaʿiyya) in 2011. The current regime has no intention of catering to any of them, instead focusing on megaprojects such as the building of the new capital, to which they are moving all government ministries and the presidential complex (Michaelson 2018) and the new Suez Canal tunnels (Ahram Online 2018), in addition to the focus on surveillance and the war on terror. As we know, there are always conflicting demands that need to be satisfied in people’s lives, and the life journey of activists, whether atheists or not, is never static. We should therefore expect ambivalence. People are constantly living through ambivalence, contradictions, and experiences of failure, as Samuli Schielke (2015) highlights in his ethnography of the before, during, and after of the 2011 political revolts in Egypt.The Cairene men in focus in this article refer to themselves as muthaqqafin, or intellectuals. They attend local coffee shops and bars in Downtown Cairo almost every evening on weekdays and nightclubs on weekends (fig. 1). Today they talk explicitly about palpable responses (their own and those of others) of affective politics, such as suspicion, depression, denial, anger, fatigue, and a sense of hopelessness that developed after the summer of 2013.The fieldwork for this project was carried out in Cairo from September 2013 to the end of January 2018 as well as during the fall of 2019. All names have been changed in light of the politically sensitive nature of the subject matter, and all other information about the interlocutors is omitted to protect their safety. I have conducted fieldwork in Egypt since 2001. All these years of lived experiences, as a woman (from young to middle age) with a “halfie” background (Scandinavian and Middle Eastern) operating under different rules, have helped me build broad networks and trust and given me access to both male and female spaces (see Winegar 2012).I employ collaboration as a research tool. The men shared their lived experiences, and we shared experiences together. I have moved with collaborators through, in, and around the cityscape as they drove, walked, traveled, and socialized. I followed how events, actions, and interpretations unfolded as a way to gain an understanding of the fluid and ambiguous material reality that people experience. I observed how men performed, protested, and claimed belonging through their body language and voices in coffee shops and bars, where I paid attention to how and to what extent the men participated in political conversations as well as how they made claims of power and status or the lack thereof.My two interlocutors, Mohamad and Ali, belong to the same political crowd of Downtown Cairenes. I met them through mutual Cairene friends, although they cannot be described as close friends. These men are Egyptian citizens who, following the current paranoid military dictatorship’s tactics to control its oppositional citizens via total repression of political bodies, have effectively been deemed enemies of the state. I selected these two accounts to show how Mohamad and Ali have different perceptions of the adhan, although both are ambivalent in their responses. At the same time, they oppose both the autocratic state and the Muslim Brotherhood.Ali is a professional musician and activist whom I met through common friends in the fall of 2017. Ali was careful to praise the food before he ate, and he thanked God after every meal. However, Ali did not pray. His dark green prayer rug hung unused over a cupboard in his bedroom, like a reminder artifact of piety. I perceived Ali as very stressed, not least because of his lack of money. He struggled every day to find gigs or day jobs to afford the basics, like food and hygiene products, and every month he had to ask his landlord for a grace period to pay the rent. Ali had called on the generosity of others too many times. People around him were tired of lending money they scarcely had for fear of not getting it back. Ali repeatedly told me that he would start to pray again once he had found balance in life. I observed that he smoked and drank a lot of hashish and alcohol, probably to cope.Music was everything for Ali. He not only performed music but listened to different genres such as reggae, jazz, or blues every day and every hour. The only rupture of these loud sounds was when the muezzin performed the call to prayer. Immediately he turned off his computer and silenced others’ profane sounds, including conversations if friends were around, and praised God explicitly. I noticed that Ali’s body movements changed as well, altering into stillness. Another changed behavior I noticed, when I was in his house during one muezzin call, was that he immediately stopped kissing his girlfriend. When I asked him why, he explained that it was forbidden to kiss during the sacred sounds of prayer.I noticed, however, that Ali experienced the sacred sounds in a conflicting way. He told me that one reason was the bad quality of many of the speakers in the cityscape and that the speakers were not synchronized. A third reason was the voices of the muezzins themselves, as their oral sacral messages were often unmusical in combination with a loud volume. As a believing Muslim, Ali seemed to experience the calls as sacral sounds, but as a talented musician, he lived through these sounds as noises. I noticed that his body language became stressed when listening to too many dissonances. It was as if he struggled and reluctantly resisted the sonic environment. It seemed as though Ali listened to sacrosanct sounds just as he listened to noise. He underscored that only muezzins with musical voices should be hired and told me once that his wish, if he had money, would be to buy excellent-quality speakers and synchronize them throughout Egypt. If we listen to Ali, we can follow how audible dissonance produced by shoddy loudspeakers, calls from multiple minarets, and the quality of the muezzin’s sonic expressions provokes irritation and intolerance, but simultaneously inhibits the listening subject as the adhan brings on a sense of the sacred. The aesthetics link up with technological transformations, which are also related to the ongoing tension of being the male subject Ali is striving to be. The noise is difficult to listen to, but it is also a daily reminder that he is not living the life a Muslim man is expected to live (failing to be a breadwinner and not praying, as well as using alcohol and drugs; see Ghannam 2013).I met Mohamad through political activist friends in 2014. Mohamad frequently attends local coffee shops and alternative bars for politically heated debates in Downtown Cairo. He sees himself as politically active, to the left, and defines himself as a secular Marxist and an intellectual. His family does not live in Cairo, and I have never met them, but Mohamad described them as strict, believing Muslims, orthodox in general, and upper middle class. I would say that through his background and upbringing, Mohamad is deeply influenced by Islam, something that is observable in his daily responses and actions. Nevertheless, it seemed as if it was very important for Mohamad to resist religion.I remember one occasion especially when the state forcefully infiltrated his body through sound. Mohamad and others were at a mutual friend’s home after a long Thursday night of bar hopping, which had ended with a stop at a popular nightclub. In the early dawn, when the muezzin called for the Friday morning prayer, Mohamad burst into a rage, shouting, “Kuss ummak” (Your mother’s cunt), as an immediate response. Mohamad listened to the sound of the muezzin as pure noise—for him, it was a noise of state violence. Maybe it was also a reminder of his past that stood in sharp contrast to his desire to make himself into the man he wanted to be.Although Mohamad always participated in intense, animated political discussions and gesticulated to underscore his standpoints—to show his status and manhood in the Downtown intellectual crowd—he was still too young and inexperienced (for example, he had not yet been detained, which was remarkable considering both his political actions and the crowd he hung out with) to be considered politically brave enough and the “manly man” he aspired to be in that milieu.Sherine Hafez (2012: 39) points out that “what the events of this uprising [2011] have revealed is that notions of masculinity undermined by a repressive regime have observably shifted the terms of the patriarchal bargain between genders and ages and between the state and its people.” The state demolishes the ability of these men to make a home, since the sonic vibrations penetrate the home’s porous walls and thereby destroy any borders between the outside and the inside. Through sound, the military state constantly reminds political activists that there is no space for alternative masculinities and no home for them in Egypt. As Filipović (2018: 214) states, when the sonic is incorporated into the analysis, the separation between the public and the private becomes contested.Farha Ghannam’s (2013) findings in Egypt reveal “the parallels people made between a proper government and a proper man: protection, support, and provision” (see, e.g., Amar 2013; Inhorn 2012; Kreil 2016; Rommel 2017; Schielke 2015). These ethnographic accounts show how sacral sounds transform into noise and how noise turns into sacral sounds. Mohamad’s and Ali’s experiences both expose immediate and embodied, albeit ambivalent, responses to the call to prayer. The sonic permeates the bodies of all men, but these urban sonic experiences are experienced differently, depending on individual and collective political bodies in relation to earlier lived experiences. In this article we can follow the ambivalent struggles and tensions of being a “proper man” in relation to both dominant gender discourses and alternative manhood. Much more research is needed to fully understand dictatorship in relation to what I tentatively define as unwanted masculinities, meaning all alternative masculinities opposing the current autocratic military regime (constructed as enemies and terrorists and suspected of a lack of loyalty to the nation) through the prism of sound.

journal: Asia-pacific Journal of Convergent Research Interchange
title: Noise Analysis of Different Duct Geometries To Identify Optimal Noise Reduction Ducts
abstract: This study was conducted to derive the optimal duct geometry for noise reduction in eVTOL (electric Vertical Take-Off and Landing) ducted fan systems.To this end, ducts were designed using various NACA (National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics) airfoil configurations (NACA 4312, 4315, 8315+4315, and 1315+4315), and CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics) analysis was performed to evaluate the impact of duct geometry on the flow around the fan.The analysis model employed the MRF (Multiple Reference Frame) technique and the k- SST (Shear Stress Transport) model based on the RANS (Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes) equations to accurately predict the complex flow behavior within the ducts.Noise analysis of the four duct geometries revealed specific noise levels for each configuration.At vertical direction Receiver 4, the measured noise levels were 79.92 dB for the NACA 4312 duct, 80.58 dB for the NACA 4315 duct, 80.73 dB for the NACA 8315+NACA 4315 duct, and 79.43 dB for the NACA 1315+NACA 4315 duct.At Receiver 5, the noise levels recorded were 75.13 dB for the NACA 4312 duct, 75.98 dB for the NACA 4315 duct, 75.16 dB for the NACA 8315+NACA 4315 duct, and 74.96 dB for the NACA 1315+NACA 4315 duct.At Receiver 6, the noise levels were measured as 71.81 dB for the NACA 4312 duct, 72.66 dB for the NACA 4315 duct, 71.74 dB for the NACA 8315+NACA 4315 duct, and 71.70 dB for the NACA 1315+NACA 4315 duct.Among the four configurations, the NACA 1315+NACA 4315 duct demonstrated superior noise reduction performance, recording an average noise reduction of 0.5-1 dB (0.6-1.5%) compared to the other configurations.In the horizontal direction, however, the noise differences between all duct configurations were negligible, with values below 0.1 dB.These results confirm that changes in duct geometry can effectively contribute to noise reduction.The findings provide fundamental data for improving noise reduction performance and optimizing eVTOL designs.Furthermore, this study has the potential to contribute to solving urban noise problems in of Urban Air Mobility (UAM) field.

journal: International Journal of Scientific Development and Research
title: Predictive Analytics Based AI Framework for Enhancing Solar Panel Efficiency
abstract: Solar photovoltaic (PV) deployments are prone to degradation in performance owing to varying weather conditions, partial shadowing and electrical anomalies. A key to address these issues lies in intelligent monitoring and forecasting methods able to construct meaning out of high volumes of operational data. To ensure accurate power prediction and system reliability this study illustrates predictive analytics framework consisting of gradient-boosted ensemble learning with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. The tool captures instantaneous and temporal behavior of PV systems by utilizing real-time Internet of Things (IoT) telemetry from solar irradiance, module temperature, voltage characteristics, and more. We apply a structured feature engineering and preprocessing pipeline to historical SCADA records, sanitizing environmental noise from the data in order to identify signal, coalescing our model learning around those signals. The methodology is assessed using a dataset of 4,213 observations in time-series cross-validation. The experimental analysis shows a high prediction capability of which the coefficient of determination is 0.968 with a root mean square error = 19.4 kW, greatly exceeding the performance of standard statistical forecast method. The findings indicate that the predictive insights provided by the proposed model can assist in detecting abnormal working conditions at an early stage, leading to preventative-based operational initiatives which deliver enhanced energy generation in situations of partial shading. System integration with Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) control helps further reduce generation losses. In a nutshell, the suggested framework stems from data-driven strategies assisting improving operational efficiency and reliability of photovoltaic energy systems thus global implementation of sustainable power generation.

title: “ Joycencore rearrived / or lots of fun again”: The Seventeenth Annual Trieste Joyce School Trieste, Italy, 30 June–6 July 2013
abstract: “Joycencore rearrived / or lots of fun again”:The Seventeenth Annual Trieste Joyce School Trieste, Italy, 30 June–6 July 2013 Ágota Márton My arrival in Trieste by train revealed the city little by little, shade by shade, canal by run. It was a gradual introduction of what was to come, and it kept changing, as the pointillist effect dissolved into solid shapes, then back to striking images. The atmosphere offered an exciting palimpsest, a fruitful terrain for creative rethinking and discussions. Dublin soundscapes, Joycetrionics, Beckettiana, textual re-mappings, the Palazzo Gopievich, Giuseppe Verdi, Via Diaz, letters and the D in “Dear,” “fun at Finnegans,” and “the voice of Joyce” are just a few highlights of the experience of the seventeenth Trieste Joyce School. Its collegial and creative environment was exciting for this newcomer. If a common symbol could be found for this year’s School, paths and patterns—already signaled by the program brochure’s design—would constitute one possibility. John McCourt’s opening lecture demonstrated overwritten and superimposed paths of the “Dublinic” Trieste. He explained how this European crossroad worked as a pseudo-canvas [End Page 427] for Dublin and how it became “la mia seconda patria” for Joyce with its exuberant cultural heritage and rich intellectual hub. The amalgam of languages (the Triestine dialect echoes in the Wake), cultures, and religions here formed a congruence with Joyce’s aspiration to become a European writer. Another pathway, adding to this motif, was that of Erik Schneider’s walking tour on the fourth day of the event, with plentiful sights of and insights into Joyce’s Trieste. We were taken to key spots and heard many intriguing stories of his life there. Clare Hutton was an early speaker at the School, and she discussed Joyce’s writing in the Little Review, reflecting on the problems and consequences of serialization, uncorrected errors (for Joyce was in Trieste at that point), and textual differences and concluding that serialization enabled Joyce to view himself as a writer dealing with the problems of censorship, his efforts toward revision propelled by a cultural antagonism. Other forms of breach of faith were tackled in Gerry Smith’s presentation that focused on Joyce’s early work. He connected Joyce’s idea of betrayal to Charles Stewart Parnell’s fate, explaining how traitorous behavior metamorphoses into a source of otherness. In Dubliners, for example, Parnell is compared to a betrayed Christ. Accordingly, Joyce was weary of the potential deceitfulness of language, and this dominated his view of the human condition. Another speaker was Laura Pelaschiar who examined the female ghosts in Dubliners, where windows divide the private from the public sphere, incomplete sentences suggest the tension between horror and fascination, and witchcraft is mirrored in the physique and gestures of some female characters. These women have an ominous significance in Joyce, since their ghostliness is portrayed in a constant cycle of indetermination. The following day, the “ghost of Joyce” was transposed into the dimensions of literary tradition. Giuliana Bendelli began by examining Joyce’s “funferal” and his “wrunes” to clarify the writer’s legacy and influence on other writers and to reveal the anxiety and, at the same time, ecstasy of that influence (FW 120.10, 19.36). After a break, Luke Thurston pursued the “legalization of the demonic” within a new kind of formation observed by Joyce. The demonic self rebels against the limits of the narrative, and there is a disjunction between different spaces of the text. On Friday, other forms of transmission were featured. First, Fritz Senn’s illustration of Joyce’s verbal brilliance focused on the writer’s “histrionics of everyday life,” where every statement is turned into a linguistic event. All the action in Ulysses takes the reader somewhere else, yet it remains a non-dramatic form that defies its actual performance. According to Senn, stage routines, elaborate stage directions, gestures, and songs intruding upon the text create a battleground for [End Page 428] conflicting discourses and competing words. It is only Bloom who does not fit in rhetorically; he is not listened to, and though he would like to perform, he is never given the chance. Other speakers reflected a change...

title: 100 Years Ago in the American Ornithologists’ Union
abstract: The 38th stated meeting of the American Ornithologists’ Union (AOU), the first of the “Roaring Twenties,” was held in Washington, D.C. Business meetings were convened on Monday, November 8, at the Cosmos Club on Lafayette Square, at the corner of Madison Place and H Street Northwest. President John H. Sage called the meeting of the Council to order at 1030 hours. Meetings of Fellows and Fellows and Members were held at The Club that evening. The 19th Amendment, ratified that summer, granted women the right to vote, but their rights remained limited. Three Members of the AOU were women: Florence Merriam Bailey, Althea Sherman, and Mabel Osgood Wright. Although no mention is made of their attendance at the meeting that night, they would not have entered through the front door (Kirgis 2006). The membership was comprised of Fellows (49), Retired Fellows (3), Honorary Fellows (19), Corresponding Fellows (75), Members (86), and Associates (910), for a total of 1,142. Meeting attendance included ~10% of membership; 25 active and 2 retired fellows were present, including 2 founders. Election of officers resulted in Witmer Stone replacing John H. Sage as President; Stone would continue as editor of The Auk. W. L. McAtee was elected Treasurer. Jonathan Dwight became Vice President alongside Vice President George Bird Grinnell. T. S. Palmer continued as Secretary. W. K. Fisher requested transfer to the list of Retired Fellows, and Frederick A. Lucas (1852–1939) took his place on the Council. During the year, the Union had lost 16 members to death, including William Dutcher (1846–1920), a Fellow. Dutcher, a lawyer by trade, was a stalwart of bird conservation. He was appointed in 1895 by William Brewster as Chairman of the Committee for the Protection of North American Birds. Dutcher mobilized the stagnant Committee to action. He composed the AOU Model Law, a template used by states to establish protections for nongame birds. He was influential in President Theodore Roosevelt’s decision to create the first of many wildlife refuges, Pelican Island National Wildlife Refuge in Florida. Integral to the relationship of the AOU with Audubon, he chaired the National Committee to organize the National Association of Audubon Societies (now National Audubon Society) and served as its first President. His many accomplishments for conservation resulted from hours spent outside his vocation. T. S. Palmer (1921) ends Dutcher’s memorial with the following: “to know William Dutcher was a privilege, to work with him was an inspiration.” No doubt it was. The opening for Fellow was filled with the election of Robert Cushman Murphy (1887–1973), an expert on oceanic birds. He would become AOU President in 1942. A voyage aboard one of the last sail-powered whaling ships influenced his work. In Logbook for Grace, detailing his voyage, he wrote, “I now belong to a higher cult of mortals, for I have seen the albatross!’’ (Murphy 1947, p. 148). His lifelong association with the American Museum of Natural History began with assistance to Frank M. Chapman (1864–1945), and resulted in his appointment as Lamont Curator of birds. He was awarded the Brewster’s Medal for Oceanic Birds of South America (Amadon 1974). Myron H. Swenk, T. C. Stephens, I. N. Gabrielson, Loye Holmes Miller, and A. A. Saunders were elected Members. Swenk (1883–1941), an entomologist with the University of Nebraska, founded the Nebraska Ornithologists’ Union and was President of the Wilson Ornithological Club. Thomas Calderwood Stephens (1876–1948), also served as President of the Wilson Ornithological Club and as editor of the The Wilson Bulletin. A staunch advocate of bird conservation, his editorials expressed views on subjects such as collecting permits, not then generally acceptable to the ornithological community (Hall 1988). Ira Noel Gabrielson (1889–1977), Stephens’ former student, was perhaps influenced by Stephens. Gabrielson, a future Fellow of the AOU (1938), reported his revelation, “When I learned that there were actually jobs where people were paid for studying birds and mammals, I knew exactly what I wanted to do.” This led his father to stop paying his tuition, but that did not stop Gabrielson from achieving a prestigious career in zoology (Reeves and Marshall 1985). He joined the Biological Survey and became the first director of the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service, expanding the National Wildlife Refuge System, and creating the Patuxent Wildlife Research Refuge. Aretas A. Saunders (1884–1970), “Father of Avian Community Ecology” (Smith 2014), based upon his publication of studies in avian community dynamics and succession, would be elected Fellow in 1950. He was also known for his interest in adding song and behavior to classification and for his method of illustrating birdsong. Of Members elected, Loye “Padre” Holmes Miller (1874–1970) was unique. Founder of Avian Paleontology in California, elected Fellow in 1930, he was a passionate educator, naturalist, storyteller, and songster. His imitations of birdsongs were known to lure birds. These, along with his stories and songs, are captured in a series of albums (Howard 1971). Collecting trips with paleontologist John C. Merriam (1869–1945) influenced his career. A portion of one fossil bird bone had been retrieved from Rancho La Brea when the 2 visited there in 1906. Miller recorded 65 species by completion of his PhD (1912), and over the course of his career at the University of California, Los Angeles, Davis, and Berkeley, he studied over 150,000 fossilized bird bones, including approximately 90 extinct species (Howard 1971, Ball et al. 1974). Two Honorary Fellows, 13 Corresponding Fellows, and 306 Associates were elected, including Margaret Morse Nice (1883–1974). Previously elected Associate in 1907, she left the Union, rejoined in 1920, and was elected Member in 1931. Proposed for Fellow twice before election in 1937, she was the second female Fellow in AOU history (Barrow 1998). She pioneered the use of colored bands for life-history studies and was awarded the Brewster Medal in 1942 for her studies on Song Sparrows (Melospiza melodia). Her work with European ethologists Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen informed her research, and she was influential in introducing ethology to the United States (Trautman 1977). She published more than 250 articles and monographs, penned 7 books, and reviewed over 3,000 publications. Strides taken by Margaret Morse Nice, while confined to the role of housewife and amateur ornithologist, would pave the way for women as professional ornithologists. Public sessions, held in the days following at the United States National Museum, included 38 presentations on topics including plumage, bird banding, nomenclature, and pronunciation. Nine were illustrated by lantern slides and 5 by motion pictures. More technical papers were presented at a special session with more time for discussion. The first Auklet, a parody of The Auk, appeared at the Meeting that year. Subtitled An Occasional Journal of Ornithological Minutia, it had no cover drawing, but had as tailpiece the backside of a bird, presumably a Great Auk, drawn by drunken and “Celebrated Danish Ornithologist, Hans Egede.” The Volstead Act had just passed and the topic of Prohibition was common in The Auklet over the next century (Parkes 1983). In 1920, its “Steenth Supplement to the AOU Checklist” suggested that Brewer’s Sparrow be renamed “Temperance Sparrow,” Brewer’s Blackbird, exhibiting “suspicious behavior,” be renamed “Home-brew Blackbird,” and it was surmised that Grinnell’s California Brewer’s Blackbird weighed less “in drams” due to its “constant state of ferment.” Unusual sightings by “Pro Bono Publico” were attributed to “Old Crow Rye.” Throughout The Auklet the previous year’s arguments and controversies were parodied, or new stories lampooned members, either identified unabashedly or provided aliases referring to their well-known idiosyncrasies, for their notable eccentricities. It seems appropriate that the 1931 volume was subtitled Dedicated to Ornithologists Who Take Themselves Too Seriously. The question is, why was The Auklet dropped? (An Auklet answer in the form of a pun just came to me.) Surely we know human failings cause us to take ourselves too seriously; the antidote, then as now, is humor. I thank Polly Lasker, Carla Dove, Tammy Peters, and Eugen Morton at the Smithsonian Institution for assistance in the search for Auklets and Alice Blackwell for her assistance with the manuscript.

journal: Journal of the American Academy of Religion
title: Greek Orthodox Music in Ottoman Istanbul: Nation and Community in the Era of Reform . By Merih Erol
abstract: During the past few decades, ethnomusicologists and anthropologists have increasingly stressed the importance of music in negotiating national, religious, and cultural identities, particularly in shaping a nation’s image (see Philip Bohlman, Music of European Nationalism, 2004) and delimiting social and religious boundaries among ethnic communities (see Martin Stokes, Ethnicity, Identity, and Music, 1994). In Greek Orthodox Music in Ottoman Istanbul, Merih Erol takes a similar approach by discussing the “highly operative” role of music in the construction of national, religious, and class identity in the Greek Orthodox community in Istanbul during the late Ottoman Empire. Erol acknowledges that it is impossible “to replicate the sounds of nineteenth-century Constantinople/Istanbul completely” (1); however, she argues that “by investigating the ideas and discourses surrounding the musical practices of the time, we can gain a sense of the soundscapes of late Ottoman Istanbul” (2). She tackles the subject by exhaustively examining archival evidence from ecclesiastical and lay sources, including newspapers, patriarchal letters and encyclicals, musical journals and periodicals, specialized treatises and essays on music, liturgical books, and collections of popular and folk songs. The chronological focus of the book is framed between the promulgation, in 1856, of the Reform Edict, initiated by the Ottoman government regarding the “equality of its subjects beyond ethnic and religious divisions” (3), and the end of the Greek-Turkish war in 1922. Promulgation of the edict aimed at reassuring the Great Powers that the Ottoman Empire would pursue the reforms that it had begun with the Tanzimat (a period of reforms in the Ottoman Empire) in 1839. This resulted in the empire’s changing position in European diplomacy, the development of new geopolitical alliances, and integration into large European-Mediterranean trade networks. These reforms brought changes to the ethnic-religious communities in Istanbul, including the Greek Orthodox Istanbulites, especially among the educated elite, since it gave them an opportunity to negotiate their cultural identity, their Byzantine heritage, and the role of traditional liturgical music, which was confronting modernity and Westernization. The book focuses on the urban setting of the educated elite, in particular the churchgoing educated Greek Orthodox elite in Istanbul, and their debates on reforming traditional church music. By taking this approach, Erol aims to “shed light on the strategies of ethnic-communal reproduction, the images of modernity and the West, and the ideas and behavior of this social class about consumption and materiality” (10). The educated elite comprised—in addition to various types of professionals, bureaucrats, and members of the bourgeoisie—the local cantors who served at the patriarchate or in the prominent churches of the city. The book is breathtaking in its scope and coverage and is organized both thematically and chronologically. It consists of six chapters, an introduction, and a conclusion. The introduction provides a synopsis of the Greek Orthodox community in Ottoman Istanbul, the role of music in reflecting the diversity of the city, and the building of ethnic identities and nations. The conclusion puts the challenges faced by Greek Orthodox musicians during the nineteenth century in a broader context, including all musical traditions of the non-Western world. It also presents a brief introduction to the state of music among ethnic minorities—including Armenians, Greek Orthodox, and Dönmes (Jewish converts to Islam)—in the post-Ottoman era. The first two chapters open with discussion of the political, social, and cultural transformations of the Ottoman Greek Orthodox community in the second half of the nineteenth century. They tackle the discourse and attitudes of the Istanbulite Greek Orthodox middle class regarding church ritual and liturgical music, considering two processes: economic change, which “not only created the Greek Orthodox middle class but also formed new class identities and markers of social differentiation”; and the articulation of a national discourse and search for a “definition of Greekness” (40). By discussing the relevance of the concept of class, Erol investigates the links between musical choice and social identity. She also discusses aspects of music professionalism in church singing and provides detailed accounts about the social and regional origins, the educational backgrounds, and the appointment and promotion paths of Greek Orthodox cantors in nineteenth-century Istanbul. The following chapters deal with nineteenth-century Greek historiography, the appropriation of Byzantium, and Ottoman Greek perceptions and interpretations of their musical heritage against these backgrounds. They examine how music was employed in reference to the Greek past and how it helped evoke collective memory and communal identity. At the same time, these chapters focus on the debates and disputes regarding the reform of liturgical music in the Greek Orthodox community in Istanbul. They examine the efforts of the cantors and the religious authority to standardize and systematize liturgical music and its instruction and demonstrate how, ultimately, the living chanting practice was employed to restore what was considered the tradition. Chapter 5 is concerned with the first decades of the twentieth century, when ethnic identities and cultural borders became increasingly asserted in the face of events, including the Ottoman-Greek war of 1897, which resulted in mass human displacement. This led to the proliferation of a distinct cultural identity by the Istanbulite Greek Orthodox community. The chapter explores the role of Istanbulite cantors in redefining Greek musical heritage and situating themselves with regard to other ethnic groups that shared Byzantine and Ottoman urban music traditions. It later addresses the politics of nation making and identity formation and discusses specific attempts to restructure music education at Greek Orthodox schools. Chapter 6 considers state surveillance and censorship of music and popular entertainment in late Ottoman Istanbul. Conflicts began to arise between the Greek Orthodox and the state authorities over different issues, including the granting of permission for charity concerts. This chapter investigates, in particular, how Ottoman authorities faced the challenge of music that allegedly expressed patriotic feelings. The text is accompanied by nine audio examples, which, as mentioned in the preface, are associated with specific passages in the book. The recordings are available on Ethnomusicology Multimedia, a web-based media program published in collaboration with Indiana University Press and Temple University Press. Each example is assigned a unique PURL (Persistent Uniform Resource Locator). Unfortunately, the audio examples are not discussed in the text, and the citations of the PURLs are not complemented by an explanation that would connect the examples to the argument. They can therefore go unnoticed and seem to be unnecessary. Although the author asserts in the introduction that the book “may disappoint those who are seeking a technical analysis of music, for its primary focus is on the experience of the ‘extramusical’ rather than on the music itself” (13), a brief discussion of the music examples would have contributed to Erol’s attempt to replicate the sounds of nineteenth-century Istanbul. This book is a great contribution to the fields of historical ethnomusicology, religious studies, ethnic studies, and Ottoman and Greek studies. It offers timely research during a critical period for ethnic minorities in the Middle East in general and Christians in particular as they undergo persecution and forced migration.

title: Nocturnal Artificial Light Exposure in Expectant Mothers and Risk of Congenital Glaucoma
abstract: Abstract Background While the impact of light pollution on human health is gaining recognition, its role in transmitting the effects of maternal exposure to the fetus remains unclear. This study is to investigate the association between exposure to artificial light at night (ALAN) during pregnancy and risk of congenital glaucoma. Methods All birth cohorts spanning from 2008 to 2011 in urban areas of South Korea, comprising over 90% of the total population, were identified in the Korean National Health Insurance database. Average levels of ALAN at the residential addresses of mothers during pregnancy were estimated using time-varying satellite data for a composite view of persistent night-time illumination at ∼1 km2 scale.The odd ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) of the association between residential ALAN and risk of congenital glaucoma - was computed using logistic regression. These calculations were adjusted for socio-demographic factors and area-level risk factors (night-time traffic noise and particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter ≤ 10 μm). Results A total of 745,458 mother-father-child trios (mean [SD] age of the mothers, 32.4 [3.8] years; 387,275 [52.0%] boy) were included in the study. In fully adjusted models, an IQR (21.8 nW/cm2/sr) increase in ALAN level was associated with an OR of 1.12 (95% CI: 1.05, 1.19) for incident congenital glaucoma. The exposure-response curve demonstrated an upward slope with a threshold at approximately 62 nW/cm2/sr. Conclusions In this nationwide population-based case-control study, higher levels of residential ALAN during pregnancy were associated with increased risk of congenital glaucoma. Future studies with more detailed information on exposure, individual adaptive behaviors and potential mediators are warranted. Key messages • This study indicates an association between elevated levels of ALAN exposure in pregnant women and a heightened risk of congenital glaucoma in their offspring. • These results are consistent with a growing body of evidence underscoring the detrimental effects of ALAN on health, reinforcing its potential role as a risk factor for congenital glaucoma.

title: Animal Histories of the Civil War Era ed. by Earl J. Hess (review)
abstract: Reviewed by: Animal Histories of the Civil War Era ed. by Earl J. Hess Jessica M. Lepler (bio) Animal Histories of the Civil War Era. Edited by Earl J. Hess. (Baton Rouge: Louisiana State University Press, 2022. Pp. 288. Cloth, $45.00.) At a conference in 2018, Earl J. Hess, author of more than two dozen books on the U.S. Civil War, attended an inspiring roundtable. Before leaving the meeting, Hess recruited two authors for a proposed volume that expanded the panel's innovation: combining the burgeoning field of animal history with the perennially booming field of Civil War studies. Hess then edited and efficiently shepherded into print a thirteen-essay volume (including three of his own essays) that aims to be "the first effort to fill" what he describes as "a gaping hole in the Civil War literature concerning [End Page 566] animals and a similar void in the work of animal historians where the Civil War ought to be" (1). Animal Histories of the Civil War Era cannot fill such a vast expanse of uncharted historical territory, but it does reveal a universe of scholarly possibilities. The book is divided into six sections that sketch both chronological and thematic arcs. After Hess's introduction, the book begins with Michael E. Wood's essay linking the antebellum importation of camels to proslavery agricultural improvers, dubious capitalists, and soon-to-be Confederate operatives. The dramatic story of these desert dromedaries in cotton country sets the stage for several themes of the volume: the long chronological reach of the era, the wide range of species involved, and the analytical tug-of-war over whether humans or animals ought to be the center of Civil War–era animal history. Turning from an exotic ungulate to the war's most iconic animals, the second section of the book features three essays on equines written by David J. Gerleman, Hess, and Abraham Gibson, respectively. Ridden into battle, hauling artillery, and captured as contraband, horses and mules were often seen as "engines" powering the war (46), but they were also sentient beings with wills of their own. Like several other resonances with earlier animal history scholarship throughout the book, this formulation offers an interesting parallel to Clay McShane and Joel A. Tarr's description of equines in nonmartial nineteenth-century settings as "living machines," powering industrializing cities.1 Integrated into many of the war's controversial monuments, horses' martial service has been the most remembered of any animal involved in the Civil War. Far from sitting atop pedestals, most animals affected by the war were beyond human control and historical memory. The third section of the book is focused on wildlife and unveils a world of unlimited historical potential. Birds, small woodland mammals, fish, and other vertebrates served as food for foraging soldiers and often experienced habitat destruction. But insects and other invertebrates—making up "98 percent" of all known animals—really change the readers' perspective on the Civil War (105). For example, the slaughter of humans, horses, and domesticated food animals became a feast for the 120,000 species of flies that inhabit what Hess calls "Civil War country" (106). The flies contributed to the unsanitary camp conditions, which supported a surge in lice, ticks, and mites. Even bees, as Mark Smith's essay argues, "occupied a surprising center" in Civil War–era history (122), as symbols of industriousness, suppliers of sweetness, and sources of the war's buzzing soundscape. Food is the subject of the book's fourth section. Jason Phillips's provocative essay redefines sectionalism through the history of hogs. Before the [End Page 567] Civil War, the North industrialized the production of pig-based meat, but southerners commanded their pigs to fend for themselves on vast expanses of common land. This latter practice, first documented by Virginia DeJohn Anderson in her foundational study of colonial animal history, reflected the divergence between Confederate persistence and Union industrialization, with significant ramifications for the conflict.2 Although their approaches to animal husbandry may have varied, the men fighting the Civil War were predominantly meat-powered. title: Gender and the Spatiality of Blackness in Contemporary AfroFrench Narratives by Polo B. Moji (review)
abstract: Reviewed by: Gender and the Spatiality of Blackness in Contemporary AfroFrench Narratives by Polo B. Moji Eric Touya de Marenne Moji, Polo B. Gender and the Spatiality of Blackness in Contemporary AfroFrench Narratives. Routledge, 2022. ISBN 978-0-3676-3751-4. Pp. 182. The book analyzes the spatiality of blackness in contemporary France through literature, film, and music as narrative forms. One of Moji's aims is to "situate the study of black spatiality outside the too familiar narrative of the banlieue" and "complicate France's myth of racial freedom" (6) anchored by Francophonie or the Hexagon. The author explores how race and gender intersect in the (re)mapping of French urban spaces. Using walking as method, her analytical framework seeks to go beyond the traditional representations of ghettoized banlieues to explore the banality of blackness in the everyday. In this Afro-French context, Moji recasts Walter Benjamin's flâneur as the black flâneuse shaped by the politics of race and gender. She argues that "the material-discursive framing of black flânerie, as both relationality and embodied movements in French spaces, renders visible the processes of place-making and recapitalization embedded in daily lives of black women" (7). Flânerie is both the site of an ethnographic gaze and a movement of relation as "AfroFrench identities as inherently relational, multiple and mobile" (8). The book is organized into two sections. In the first one entitled "The long shadow of Marianne," Moji puts into dialogue works like Calixthe Beyala's Lettre d'une Afro-française à ses compatriotes that address the systemic exclusion of minorities as a failure of French republican values. Cecile Emeke's Flâner, Pascale Obolo's short film, La femme invisible, and Mame-Fatou Niang's web documentary Mariannes noires are placed in conversation to reveal black women's invisibility in French media space. Through Diome's collection of essays Marianne porte plainte!, her autobiographical short story collection La préférence nationale, and her novel titled Le ventre de l'Atlantique, Moji explores the exclusion of the racialized subject and the self-reflexive narrative of the errant writer. Finally, in a chapter entitled "Black or French: Voicing the borders of black France," Moji problematizes the ethnocentric conception of French identity through Léonora Miano's Marianne et le garçon noir, Écrits pour la parole, and Habiter la frontière. In the second section of the book entitled "Blackness intra muros," Moji analyzes the concept of "Afropeanism" which connotes a post-occidental and post-racist utopia through Léonora Miano's novel Blues pour Élise and Édouard Glissant's Poétique de la relation. Originating from the music of Zap Mama and Miano's literary transposition, the rhizomic/relational schema of "Afropeanism" introduces the reader to Parisian soundscape of Blackness. To close the section, Moji explores in "Reimagining AfroParisianism: Blackness encoded; spatiality decoded" the encoding of globalized blackness through [End Page 136] hip-hop culture in French space. Moji's ground-breaking book highlights the persistence of the geographic collusion that the presence of Black bodies creates and how it disrupts the "fixation of French homogeneity" (45). It is a compelling addition to emerging contemporary Black French studies and demonstrates the need for ongoing transatlantic and afro-diasporic research about blackness in a French context.
