title: MANUFACTURERS NEWS
abstract: New approach to ear hygiene GARDEN CITY PARK, NY—Hal-Hen Company, Inc., (www.halhenpro.com) is presenting a new approach to ear hygiene, the Murine® Earigate™ Ear Cleansing System. Designed and tested by an ENT physician, Earigate helps keep ears clean longer. Using patented “reverse spray action,” the product safely rinses away earwax and cellular debris without putting pressure on the tympanic membrane.FigureHal-Hen notes that the easy-to-use system widens the time between ear cleanings and helps prevent hearing aid failure due to wax or debris buildup. Clinically tested, Earigate™ is free of chemicals and preservatives, is hypoallergenic, and can be used as often as necessary. It comes in two sizes: adult and child. Each 100 ml can deliver 30 to 50 applications. Clarity spreads word about hearing loss NASHVILLE—More than 40 country music stars teamed up with Clarity and The EAR Foundation during the Academy of Country Music (ACM) Awards on May 15 to bring attention to the growing problem of hearing loss and also to help raise money for disabled veterans. Country music artists were asked to help the cause by autographing a donated Takamine guitar at the ACM Awards. The guitar is being displayed in a traveling exhibit going to 21 Disabled American Veterans (DAV) air shows throughout the summer to raise funds to support DAV's service and outreach for veterans. Among the musicians who signed the guitar are Sara Evans, Vince Gill, The Wreckers, Eddie Montgomery and Troy Gentry of Montgomery Gentry, Sugar Land, and Miranda Lambert. Clarity, a division of Plantronics, Inc. (www.plantronics.com), and a major producer of amplified telephones, and The EAR Foundation, a non-profit organization devoted to education, prevention, and treatment of hearing loss, have attended the ACM Awards for the past 3 years, raising awareness of hearing loss and donating products to help musicians who suffer from noise-induced hearing loss.Figure: Helping raise hearing awareness and care for disabled veterans are, from left, Daniel Claire of the Disabled American Veterans (DAV); country musicians Michelle Branch and Jessica Harp of the Wreckers; and Chris Dutton of Clarity.“Our goal as a company is to provide solutions that improve a person's quality of life,” said Chris Dutton of Clarity. “It is our hope that we, along with some of country music's greatest artists, will be able to help The EAR Foundation and DAV raise awareness and funds to help improve the lives of those they serve.” CareCredit adds features COSTA MESA, CA—CareCredit has added new features and functionality to CareCredit.com designed to give practices immediate access to reports and information that can help them manage the financing portion of their practice and successfully encourage patients to seek optimal hearing care. Using Activity At-A-Glance, CareCredit Summary, and Cardholder Availability Lookup, hearing professionals can access account activity and transaction history during the past 15 months as well as view patients' available credit. Phonak implements new DSL standard STFA, SWITZERLAND—The new pediatric fitting rationale DSL v5 is now available in the newest release of the Phonak Fitting Guideline iPFG1.7. DSL was originally developed for infants and children with hearing impairment. However, DSL v5 not only offers significant improvements in pediatric fittings, but also extends the benefits of DSL to adult fittings. Innovations include compatibility with ABR measurements, up-dates to age-related real-ear-to-coupler difference (RECD) values, and different targets for listening in quiet and in noise. The Phonak implementation of DSL v5 was accomplished in close cooperation with the DSL experts at the University of Western Ontario (UWO). The Phonak implementation in iPFG1.7 enables fitters to use DSL v5 with all Phonak hearing instruments. Advanced technology, at all price points and in a wide variety of models, can thus be chosen without limitation. FM user guides adapted for visually impaired FM products from Phonak are used by an increasing number of hearing-impaired adults, many of whom also have visual impairments. Therefore, Phonak has prepared a set of specially adapted user guides for those with vision problems. To read comfortably, visually impaired people require high-level contrast and large 14- or 16-point fonts. The newly adapted user guides from Phonak fulfill these requirements. Available in 10 languages, the guides can be downloaded as PDF files from the Phonak web site and will also be embedded in Phonak's fitting software for FM products. Phonak reports higher sales, profit The Phonak Group has reported that sales in financial year 2006/2007 increased by 23.8% to reach CHF 1.073 billion, compared with CHF 866.7 million the year before. Internal growth came to 16.1%. Phonak reported that its gross profit margin climbed by 1.6% to 68.2% and that operating profit (EBITA) increased by 32.6% to CHF 283.6 million from CHF 213.9 million in 2005/2006. The EBITA margin reached 26.4%, up from 24.7% in the previous financial year. Looking ahead, Phonak says that the delay in completing the agreed-to acquisition of ReSound “is annoying, but will not impact our strategy or competitiveness in any way. We are confident that Phonak Group's sales will continue to develop in line with our mid-term target to grow the company by around 10% on an annual basis.” The acquisition has been delayed by a ruling, now being appealed, of the German Federal Cartel Office. Energizer survey finds few get hearing tested ST. LOUIS—More than 28 million Americans have hearing loss, including many in their 50s and 60s. However, for many in this age group, avoiding questions about their hearing is as common as avoiding the fact that they are getting older. According to a new Healthy Hearing survey conducted for Energizer (www.energizer.com), more than two out of three respondents (67.1%) said they were concerned about hearing loss, but only 30% felt it was important to get their hearing checked. Furthermore, only 11.5% have had their hearing tested in the past year. The survey, which polled men and women ages 50 to 70, was part of Energizer's new Healthy Hearing campaign, which kicked off in May during Better Hearing and Speech Month. One goal of the program is to encourage people to get their hearing checked and inform them about the professionals who diagnose hearing loss. More than 70% of respondents to the survey said they would consult an internist or family doctor about hearing loss, but only 44% said they would consult an audiologist. “Some studies have shown that only 14% of physicians routinely screen for hearing loss during a physical,” said Michael Valente, PhD, director of adult audiology at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. “Since most people with hearing impairment hear well in a quiet environment like a doctor's office, it can be virtually impossible for a physician to recognize the extent of a patient's problem. Without special training and an understanding of hearing loss, it may be difficult for a doctor even to realize that he or she has a hearing problem.” Valente hopes the Energizer Healthy Hearing program will help clear up many of the misconceptions people have about hearing loss, which the survey demonstrates. For example, 38.2% believe hearing aids will make them feel old, and 36.8% think wearing a hearing aid will be uncomfortable. Packaging innovation launched Energizer has introduced a new type of packaging for its hearing aid batteries. The new packaging, in which each battery is individually sealed and perforated, replaces the spin pack. It is designed to make using batteries easier and more convenient for hearing aid wearers. Energizer cited advantages of individually sealed batteries: Coins and other metal objects won't touch batteries, avoiding short-outs. Users can take one or two batteries with them and leave the rest of the pack behind. Also, according to the company, the new longer and wider tabs make inserting batteries into hearing aids easier. Room-within-a-room launched at AAA DENVER—DigiCare Hearing Research (www.digicare.org) of Colorado City, CO, introduced a lightweight, acoustically treated sound enclosure for use in clinics, at health fairs, mall shows, and wherever sound levels need to be controlled for hearing test purposes. The new anechoic units disassemble into two sections weighing approximately 68 pounds each. Assembled, the unit is small enough to fit through a 30-inch doorway.Figure“This is the first portable, low-cost sound control unit that assures an adequate sound environment that can be taken from location to location with minimal effort,” stated Max Chartrand, PhD, president of DigiCare. Avada reports growth LOUISVILLE—Avada Audiology & Hearing Care Centers (www.avada.com), the operating subsidiary of Hearing Healthcare Management, Inc. (HHM), reported strong gains in net sales and profits from operations for the first quarter of 2007. Steve Barlow, Avada's CEO and chairman of the board of managers of HHM, said. “We are on target in meeting our goals for sales growth and profitability for 2007.” Nationwide, Avada reported that net sales increased by 14.4% in Q1 2007 over Q1 2006, primarily driven by organic sales. The company reported that first-quarter profits rose by 201% year to year. Avada plans to expand the Avada Member Group program, designed for individuals who do not necessarily want to sell their practice but want to build their practice to its maximum value. The company's expansion activities are also continuing. Said Barlow, “We are seeking high-quality practice owners whose philosophies and practice standards mirror our own.” Avada operates more than 200 hearing healthcare centers nationwide. Information on membership is available from the national coordinators, Russell Hearn and John Bartolucci, at 800/216-1185 or at www.avada.com. Ultrasonic cleaner offered DALLAS—Sy Kessler Sales, Inc. (www.sykessler.com) has announced that it is offering the GemOro 1.2 Quart Ultrasonic Cleaner. The all-black ultrasonic cleaning machine features a contemporary design and is constructed out of durable ABS plastic. It has a capacity of 1.2 quarts, which is suitable for most cleaning applications. The device cleans earmolds, testing tips, and specula and removes dirt and grime from most items in minutes.FigureBeltone holds annual meeting ORLANDO—Beltone held its 2007 Annual Meeting here at the Renaissance Orlando Resort at SeaWorld March 1–3. The meeting, themed “The Journey… Good to Great,” attracted more than 800 members of the Beltone network, including 106 international guests from 18 countries. Hearing care practitioners from around the world gather at Beltone's annual meeting to share ideas, participate in educational seminars, and learn about the company's newest products and services. Todd Murray, president, Beltone USA, congratulated all the company's network members for their achievements. The company recognized a number of outstanding dispensers for their efforts. Beltone presented its most prestigious award, the President's Cup, to Michael Andreozzi of Warwick, RI, for exceptional patient care, community involvement, and professional business practices. In addition, Georgean Barden of East Pointe, MI, received Beltone's 2006 Cornerstone Award, which recognizes individuals who have exemplified strong leadership qualities within the Beltone network and in their community. In 2001, she and her son, Randy, shared the President's Cup Award. Sadly, on March 31, Georgean Barden died at age 77. She was survived by her brothers, James and Robert; her sister, Dorinda; her children, Larrry, Pam, Jim (Debra), JoAnne (Scott), and Randy (Marie-Therese); and four grandchildren. Her family has suggested that any memorial contributions be made to the American Cancer Society, the Unity East Church; 23057 N. Nunneley Road, Clinton Township, MI 48036; or the Association for Research and Enlightenment, 215 67th St., Virginia Beach, VA 23451. Med-El builds a bridge DURHAM, NC—Med-El Corporation (www.medel.com) has launched Bridge to Better Communication, a program for hearing professionals, schools, and coch-lear implant users and their parents to help close the gap between implantation and the development of improved listening skills and spoken communication. Bridge consists of a wide variety of products, resources, and tools for adult and pediatric habilitation, assessment, and device management, including the recently released My LittlEars Diary and the LittlEars Auditory Questionnaire. LittlEars materials are designed to assess age-appropriate auditory behavior of pre-verbal children. Many of the resource materials are available at no charge and can be downloaded for instant access. Technicians certified by NASED DENVER—The National Association of Special Equipment Distributors (NASED) has accounced the certification of four new NASED technicians: Mike Wood from Gordon N. Stowe and Associates, Inc.; Alan Snow and Leo Boguslawski from Medical Technologies, Inc.; and Shad Robinson from MSR West, Inc. The four all passed the NASED Certification Examination given at AudiologyNOW! in April in Denver. AHAA provides benchmarking data WEST CHESTER, PA—American Hearing Aid Associates (AHAA) has begun offering financial and other information to its national network of member associates that allow an owner/manager to compare the performance of his or her practice with that of comparable practices in the industry as a whole as well as with others in the AHAA network. Called the ExecuTrak Reporting System, this service provides performance data by type of practice ownership (audiologist, ENT, and hearing aid specialist) in four practice sizes ranging from under $250,000 to more than $1 million in annual sales. The data are presented for 14 benchmarks, including gross units sold, average sale price, gross margin, closure rate, return rate, resell rate, and percentage of operating expense to sales. The data for the AHAA network are submitted confidentially by associates for their own practices. The ExecuTrak Reporting System allows associates to create specific plans to improve a practice's performance based on how it compares with industry and AHAA averages. AHAA (www.ahaanet.com) publishes an annual ExecuTrak Report that provides aggregated information for the industry and for AHAA practices. It includes an analysis of strong and weak points for both segments.

title: Quantum leap: Exploring uncharted territories in ophthalmology with a wink and a qubit
abstract: Dear Editor, As quantum computing (QC) rapidly progresses, its potential applications in ophthalmology could revolutionize the field. To the best of my knowledge, this innovative concept has not been explored in ophthalmology before. The intersection of QC and eye care can lead to a significant shift, offering transformative solutions that could enhance the diagnosis, treatment, and comprehension of ocular diseases. QC shows immense potential for various compute-intensive health-care tasks, particularly within the interconnected digital health realm influenced by the Internet of Things. What exactly is QC? Imagine regular computing as solving math problems step by step, one after another. Classical computers use bits as the basic unit of information, represented as either 0 or 1. Now, contrast this with QC: quantum computers utilize quantum bits, or qubits, which can exist in multiple states simultaneously due to superposition. In essence, QC is akin to solving all those problems at once, occurring simultaneously rather than sequentially. While classical computers follow a linear path, quantum computers explore multiple paths concurrently, completing calculations in a massively parallel manner.[1] Some processes used in QC are as follows:[2] Superposition: Qubits can represent both 0 and 1 simultaneously, enabling quantum computers to perform many calculations in parallel. This vastly increases their processing power compared to classical computers. Entanglement: Another key principle of quantum mechanics, entanglement, allows qubits to become correlated with each other in such a way that the state of one qubit instantly influences the state of another, regardless of the distance between them. This property enables quantum computers to perform complex operations and solve certain types of problems much more efficiently than classical computers. Quantum gates: Quantum computers use quantum gates to manipulate qubits and perform operations. These gates, such as Hadamard gates and Controlled NOT (CNOT) gates, can create and manipulate superpositions and entanglements, allowing quantum algorithms to be executed. Quantum algorithms: Algorithms designed specifically for quantum computers take advantage of superposition and entanglement to solve certain problems exponentially faster than classical algorithms. For example, Shor’s algorithm for factoring large numbers and Grover’s algorithm for searching unsorted databases are two famous examples of quantum algorithms that demonstrate the potential power of QC. Quantum error correction: Quantum systems are susceptible to errors due to environmental noise and imperfections in hardware. Quantum error correction techniques, such as encoding qubits in larger quantum codes and implementing error-correcting quantum gates, are crucial for preserving the integrity of quantum computations. Some potential applications of QC include the following:[2,3] QC holds transformative potential across various domains of healthcare and medicine. It can significantly accelerate DNA sequencing, revolutionizing personalized medicine by enabling the development of tailored therapies and medications through detailed modeling. Moreover, QC promises to enhance imaging systems, offering clinicians unprecedented clarity in real-time diagnostics. In the realm of cancer treatment, QC can address complex optimization problems in devising precise radiation therapy plans, ensuring targeted destruction of cancerous cells while preserving healthy tissues. In addition, QC facilitates the in-depth study of molecular interactions at their fundamental levels, advancing drug discovery and medical research. The use of quantum bits (qubits) can expedite whole-genome sequencing and analytics, potentially completing these tasks in significantly reduced time frames. Furthermore, QC can enhance in silico clinical trials, which involve entirely computer-simulated testing of therapies or drugs. Although completely simulated trials are not yet feasible due to current limitations in biological understanding, they offer significant advantages over traditional in vivo trials.[4] Some examples showcasing QC being used in healthcare are as follows: Sengupta and Srivastava[5] developed a quantum algorithm to expedite the clinical prognostic analysis of coronavirus disease 2019 patients. They utilized quantum machine learning algorithms, stemming from QC theory, for machine learning tasks, leveraging solution parallelism. Their approach demonstrated efficient quantum simulation and rapid convergence, particularly in large-scale, biased, computed tomography-scanned image classification. Hussain et al.[6] devised a multiobjective quantum-inspired genetic algorithm to address healthcare deadline scheduling challenges. Recognizing the critical implications of missing deadlines in healthcare, their algorithm models health-care applications as workflows represented by directed cyclic graphs. Individual tasks within the workflow are assigned deadlines to ensure the quality of service. Proposed uses of QC in healthcare[2] Liu et al. proposed a logistic regression health assessment model using quantum optimal swarm optimization for early disease detection. In the field of imaging, Javidi reviewed research on 3D visualization techniques and quantum imaging under photon-starved conditions, suggesting notable improvements in visualization. Childs et al. explored the use of cloud-based quantum computers for natural language processing on electronic health-care data, potentially transforming data analysis in healthcare. Datta et al. developed a mobile app, “Aptamers for Detection and Diagnostics,” which utilizes optical data from conjugated quantum nanodots to detect molecules indicative of the sever acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2. Koyama et al. proposed a midinfrared spectroscopic system employing a pulsed quantum cascade and high-speed wavelength-swept laser for health-care applications, including blood glucose measurement. In addition, Naresh et al. suggested a quantum DH extension for dynamic quantum group key agreement in multiagent systems-based e-healthcare applications within smart cities, enhancing the security and efficiency of digital health solutions. Proposing some uses of QC in ophthalmology QC holds significant promise for applications in ophthalmology as well. The intricate nature of vision and the complexities underlying eye diseases demand a level of computational power that surpasses current capacities. QC can help us in enabling simulations of retinal processes, deciphering genetic predispositions to eye conditions, and optimizing personalized interventions tailored to individual patient needs. Imagine a scenario where quantum-enabled models simulate the behavior of light particles within the eye, aiding in the development of advanced imaging techniques surpassing the limitations of existing technologies. Picture quantum-based algorithms assisting in the swift and precise analysis of retinal scans, allowing for earlier detection of diseases like glaucoma or macular degeneration, potentially preventing irreversible vision loss. However, as we delve into this uncharted territory, challenges abound. The integration of QC into the clinical setting demands concerted interdisciplinary efforts, bridging the expertise of quantum physicists, computer scientists, and ophthalmologists. Moreover, the necessity for robust quantum hardware, error correction mechanisms, and the ethical implications of handling sensitive patient data necessitate careful consideration and collaborative dialog. In conclusion, while the realization of QC’s full potential in ophthalmology may be on the horizon, it requires concerted efforts, resource allocation, and collaborative partnerships. Embracing this transformative technology holds the promise of reshaping the landscape of eye care, ushering in an era where precision, efficiency, and personalized treatments converge for the betterment of global ocular health. title: Intoning the Male and Female Voices in a Novel by Eva Figes
abstract: The book Light, with Monet at Giverny: A Novel is a story that imaginatively describes a day in the life of the Monet family. It is written by one of the feminist writers of the first wave which ended in the seventies, “Simone de Beauvoir, Betty Friedan, Eva Figes, Germaine Greer, Shulamith Firestone, and Kate Millett”,1 as described by Susan Watkins in Twentieth Century Women Novelists: Feminist Theory into Practice. Watkins' book describes these women as being opposed to contemporary interpretations of Freudian theory, and in particular to certain aspects of his description of the Oedipus complex which they see as patriarchal and arising from capitalist values2 and the hypothesis that hysteria is self-motived rather than a problem of sexuality.3 Yet what Sally Robinson recognizes in Engendering the Subject: Gender and Self-representation in Contemporary Women's Fiction4 as the refreshing plurality of the voices of these feminist authors is characteristic as well of those who remain faithful to religion or Christianity, which are traditionally feminine voices. This paper searches for the developing voice of women in this work of fiction by Eva Figes and recognizes as well the presence of the continuing male voices. A positive aspect of Figes' novels is the fact that she often finds a way for a character to thrive despite harsh conditions.Throughout the novel, exterior sounds such as a clock counting the hours, a nearby passing train, singing birds and galloping horses create some sonorous effects. As the land lies amongst hills and a river, echoes can also be heard. These sounds punctuate the dialogues and silences within which much of the meaning of the story is contained. In this novel about an artistic family, the auditory effects are enhanced by visual motifs of light and color. In another of her novels, The Knot, there is a similar recurrence of ‘[n]ot merely sound, but now light, coming and going‘.5 Light follows human voices and activities that accompany the passing of the daytime sun. However, if the auditory and visual effects in The Knot may be broadly attached to hallucinations, in the present novel under discussion, light and sound come from natural sources, and indeed for the patriarch of the family, the visual artist Claude Monet, the sun is central to his creativity. The title of the novel is an obvious allusion to his life and work.The writer Octave Mirbeau (1848–1917) described in 1889 Monet's Impressionist style of painting that portrayed light and water as if they were contained in an envelope.6 Mirbeau also appears as a character in Figes' novel. The theme of visual art within a literary work requires that the art leave within the reader a sentimental or existential impression. The critic Sally Robinson discusses the impact of painting as a subject for a novel and concludes that the visual effect replaces the word as subject.7 Monet was an artist who chose to reproduce the natural world rather than imaginatively create a new image, such as accomplished by his successors such as Picasso and by Courbet, a predecessor who in 1854 painted his studio as L'Atelier, Real Allegory Determining a Phase of Seven Years of my Artistic Life. In rephrasing a comment of Julian Barnes, Robinson discusses the artistic motivation behind naturalistic painting and imaginative portraits, which “ helps answer the question of why Courbet is painting a landscape in his studio rather than en plein air: Because he is doing more than reproducing the known, established world, he is creating it himself. From now on, the painting says, it is the artist who creates the world rather than God.”8 Monet creates a new world within the context of what he sees outside. This model of mirroring the outside world is also seen in the minds of the characters who we realize are experiencing existential and personal doubt at an historical time when the Great War was approaching and the social mood was cautious. One hoped for a God and interiorly fought an increasing despair in man's ability to live peacefully together. Using Robinson's analysis, we can probe further into the atmosphere of the volatility of the historical period before the war by considering Monet's obsession with painting water lilies. Describing visual art in a novel allows the author to replace character development with thoughtful imagery and Robinson therefore sees novels about art as innovative in that they are more representative of a narration of thought than a narration of action, more about words and their ability to communicate than about character.9 Water lilies being the subject of Monet's painting at Giverny, Figes narrates how he painted a beautiful yet fragile plant slimly anchored to the bottom of a pond, a representation of beauty in arrested motion, as in Keat's “Ode to a Grecian Urn.”When making note of the use of auditory voices and silence in the novel's characters, we are indebted to Paul Ricoeur's writing about narrative and identity. Ricoeur has noted that such common auditory effects as the spoken dialogue, the monologue and silence are generally understood to emanate from a coherent communicating being. In Light, three outside voices heard are those of the author, a narrator and the author's persona, the gender of the two latter voices being ambiguous. An aesthetic discourse of abstract imagery occurs between the beings at Giverny. There are occasional direct and indirect allusions to traditional voices of poetry and prose such as William Carlos Williams, Hermann Heine, Jewish exilic authors and the novelist Charlotte Brontë. The polite predicatability of ongoing dialogues has a static effect, as if it follows patterns that have long existed and is as anchored as the water lilies. The stylistics of the voice effects are interesting and perhaps merely that. Brian Richardson has commented that it is unreasonable to assume that an innovative use of voice in a novel implies an ideological stance.10 When voices paint a sound picture it shows an aesthetic style with little ideological content.Yet Figes is interested in ethical issues of peace and conflict. Since many of the characters are often silent, can we judge them to be ethical people living in a truthful society? As Monet paints, he contemplates the scenery in silence and certain women in the story choose to remain silent within the traditional feminine social role. The reason for the women's silence may be seen in their felt need to not misrepresent what they deem necessary to say. Emma Smith in the journal Contemporary Women's Writing draws to out attention a quotation from the critic Andrew Gibson regarding silence and truth. While encouraging us to read Spinoza on this topic, Gibson says of truth and knowledge that “In the context of [a Levinasian] ethics for which ethical and epistemological questions are inseparable, distinctions between modes of narration are also the crucial ethical distinctions.”11 Spinoza, in his writing “On miracles” states that the story of a miracle is written to “inspire wonder”12 and that therefore we should consider who is describing a miracle and what we know about that person when we evaluate its real or its metaphorical value. Can such a novel with its long silences express ethical statements about war and tragedy? The search for truth lies within the domain of ethics, a traditionally male pursuit and the male conversation in the novel is unhesitatingly straightforward, in contrast to the female voice.The narrators are less so and her male narrator, Monet, as well as many of the female characters intentionally mask their critical attitudes, towards others as well as towards art and given Gibson's analysis, a writer using a supposedly omniscient narrator or a narrator with a partial knowledge of the facts or with a desire to write only through metaphor could sow confusion through a deliberate omission or an unexplained contradiction. The writer may be motivated to be silent on certain things and so to conceal events in order to complicate the plot and render the narration more interesting or he or she may judge them to be extraneous to the point. Finally, he or she may wish to avoid social or political repercussions. A similar scenario of withholding knowledge and opinions presents itself in Winter Journey when a critically important situation involving the female character becomes a visually provocative event represented by the sign : ‘The folder at the bottom of the bed said NOT TO BE EXAMINED BY THE PATIENT.'13 When reading Spinoza, one realizes that the philosopher recognized just such a necessary ethical constraint when a writer of fiction is deciding what to write about in describing hope and miracles and what to leave out. Eva Figes writes with a plurality of voices, from marginalized women whose voices are often muted, or from superior men, and to borrow an expression from Emma Smith, she values a ‘democracy of title: Listening, Elsewhere and Otherwise
abstract: A visionary keynote accompanied by an expansive pop-music mixtape played in real time, Shana L. Redmond’s presidential address at the American Studies Association’s conference in New Orleans in late 2022 imaginatively explored the soundtracks and listening practices that might plausibly have enlivened and sweetened the “unremarkable, expansive moments of repair, diplomacy, curiosity, and affection” that preceded historical instances of anti-Black police violence. Alongside erudite discussions of topics ranging from Black motoring to AM radio, the talk, titled “The Dark Prelude,” proposed an experimental, speculative listening-with as a method for insisting on the vitality of “Black living as a visionary rehearsal for futures assembled over lifetimes.” The Five Satins’ buttery-smooth “In the Still of the Nite,” Roberta Flack’s introspective “Killing Me Softly with His Song,” Gladys Knight and the Pips’ yearning “Neither One of Us (Wants to Be the First to Say Goodbye),” Leon Bridges’s mournful saxophone-twined “Sweeter”: these songs, among others, faded up and reverb’d away between the paragraphs of Redmond’s talk as her collaborator and friend Kwame Phillips activated the clips, sonically inviting the audience into scenes of quotidian tenderness and attention that were amplified by the address.The text of Redmond’s talk was first published in American Quarterly last year, where it was joined by vital responses from Erica R. Edwards and Kimberly Juanita Brown. Their short essays highlighted how Redmond’s talk entailed “a collaborative listening,” one “where to hear in detail is to grieve in detail the lives these scenes index,” while also locating itself in “the thick Black anterior, where what comes and lies before the black death that preconditions white life…is held and holding, and beheld and beholding” (Edwards 220, 219, 220); and how the talk, as a presidential address to an academic association, constituted a “scholarly engagement steeped in the ethics of care” and staked out “an enclosure—a circular refrain where what was lost could conceivably be found” that “emphasiz[ed] the multivalent possibilities for American studies” (Brown 227, 226).With this recognition of contributions to American studies and Black study still ringing in our ears, we can also pick up on another invitation in the resounding musicality of Redmond’s address: a call to a conversation that takes sound and music, especially popular music, as key points of departure and areas for exploration. In light of this, and of the impact Redmond’s scholarship (including Anthem: The Sound of Solidarity in the African Diaspora [2013] and Everything Man: The Form and Function of Paul Robeson [2020]) has had on popular music studies, JPMS invited a group of scholars who work on popular music to engage with the multimedia texts of Redmond’s talk. The forum participants contributed their annotations to a shared online document, responding both to the talk and to each other. In so doing, they created a crackling network of sonic attunement that investigates what deep and intimate attention to popular music can turn up in Redmond’s intervention, an intervention that has grown no less urgent in the months since its clarion call was first sounded.—Sara Marcus“Dark Prelude”: A Preliminary Playlist (In Order of Appearance)I cry a lot for what I’m learning and those things that I’m being forced to acknowledge that I already knew. I’m in the throes of something risky; every nerve has risen to the surface. Paper cuts draw blood, a pinprick might bring me to my knees. Devastation has become a companion, and for its presence “I [, like Kendrick,] grieve different.” The inventory that I’m tasked with is composed of the deleted details of kin. Reading their names is enough for the corners of my mouth to turn down, inhalations through my nose to quicken, my cheeks wet. This too is a part of my process; navigation of Black Study’s thick emotion.The work tonight is not an indictment of the state of the field. Like the 2022 CFP, it is an indictment of the state of the world [1] and the state of our hearts. It’s about the feelings of desire and need that guide our pens without concern for the gatekeepers and their aspirants who lie in wait. It’s about what the work forces us to do and forces us to become. When you write, do you laugh a lot, love a lot, tear up a lot, liberate a lot, take cues from emcees a lot, think about the people not on the page a lot, find wonder in it a lot, get hot with anger a lot, play a lot, create a better world a lot? Are those who haunt your thought hours pleased or furious for the truth you’ve told? Do you live with them as they live with you?[1] Matthew D. MorrisonThe use of this phrase “state of the world” also conjures Janet Jackson’s 1989 album, Rhythm Nation. title: “Queer Sonic Fingerprint”—Listening to speculative queer relations in ethnographic collections
abstract: Queer Sonic Fingerprint is the multimodal result of a collaboration between anthropologist Isabel Bredenbröker and sound artist Adam Pultz Melbye. Our work embarked from the question of how the sonic as a register of making and experiencing can inform queer relations in the context of ethnographic collections. You are listening to audio recorded during a sound installation at Art Laboratory Berlin on November 4, 2024 (120 min, assembled from a take of 4 h). The installation features sounds of artifacts in private possession and from ethnographic collections in different European museums. These have been created with a recording technique that generates a short sound called an impulse response. The sound of an impulse response is reminiscent of striking or knocking on a material body (think of drumming, a door knock, or a woodpecker). Through this process, the acoustic properties of the object's body become audible. In other words, if you knock on wood, the wood has a particular “wood” sound. If you knock on metal, so does the metal. Those sounds are defined by the specific shape and material constitution of the body from which they derive. A metal sheet, for example, will sound different to a metal tube. In addition, you are hearing bits of ambient recordings from exhibition spaces and storages at ethnological museums. You are also hearing recorded bits of conversations with curators of those collections and with people (a mix of artists and researchers) who have been part of the research process. Some of these recordings are filtered, which means that they will sound different from the original recording. This is because the recording is being played back through one of the impulse responses. In a sense, you are therefore hearing these recordings from the perspective of an artifact. You can listen to the recording here (streaming in website): https://rs.cms.hu-berlin.de/tfj/plugins/api_resource/?ref=5&k=06f07871e5. A catalogue of 45 different artifacts comprises the sonic ancestors of the sounds heard in the installation. To produce these recordings, we had to get physical access to collections. This is not easy, as such work may only be conducted in coordination with, and under the watch of a curator, possibly also a conservator. Hence, accessing collections and explaining the project to curators were a major task in the production of our work. Another challenge was the fact that we had to touch and vibrate artifacts to record them—something that sparked many questions and concerns about the integrity of the artifacts. After we developed an interface for the recording (Melbye, 2025b) that allowed us to instantly listen back to the impulse response, we experienced that curators and conservators were happy to engage in listening, often expressing surprise at the sounds revealed through the recording process. How does one, for instance, imagine the condensed resonant identity of a glass of cola nuts? How about the sound of a turtle shell or a teapot (see Figures 1-3)? To generate an impulse response (the percussive sounds you are hearing), we have used what is called the swept sine method. For this, we place a contact speaker and a contact microphone on an object (see Figures 4 and 5). Through the contact speaker, we play a sine wave, the frequency of which travels from 20 to 20,000 Hz (the approximate range of human hearing) over several seconds. The contact microphone records how the sine wave sweep sounds through the artifact. Due to the artifact's shape and material, this will sound different from the original sine wave sweep. For example, a large gong would resonate for a long time at specific frequencies, while a soft object like a fabric doll would mostly reproduce low frequencies and sound acoustically quite “dead.” Now we have two recordings: the original “pure” sine wave sweep, and the sweep as heard through the artifact. We then remove the original sine wave sweep from the recording of the object. This leaves us with a representation of just the acoustic fingerprint of that object, or what is called the Frequency Response. Finally, we perform what is called an inverse fast fourier transform on the frequency response, which produces the impulse responses you are hearing. For a more detailed discussion of this process, see Adam's work on producing the installation Kin (Melbye, 2025a). We started our collaborative conversation in early 2022. Isabel was about to embark on a research project, situated at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, that would investigate what queer methods around ethnographic collections could be. In a paper on queering ethnographic collections (Bredenbröker, 2024), Isabel engages with this question in depth. There are two takeaway points from the paper which proved relevant for our collaborative work. Firstly, queer methods are yet to be successfully applied in the context of ethnographic collections. While they are more present in museum contexts that already include queer positions, ethnographic collections are at the very start of such a possible process. Secondly, kin relations became a central theme of our thought process. More precisely, we addressed the question of how non-normative forms of kinship may be found and created in collection contexts. Here, we embarked from Alfred Gell's art nexus model, which posits non-authoritative relationality at the center of art works. Isabel had previously worked with field recording while Adam's PhD (Melbye, 2023) involved an auto-ethnography of instrument building and performance practice. Combined, this laid the foundation for an interdisciplinary multimodal work that engages with sound. We worked with interview, conversation and location recordings from museum spaces. In addition, Adam created a bespoke genetic algorithm. This software would become our collaborator for sonically amplifying possible queer kin relations between collection artifacts and their speculative descendants. In a time where the indiscriminate and uncritical use of AI and machine learning has become ubiquitous, we seized the opportunity to direct a critical gaze at the field of autonomous algorithms. Genetic algorithms were primarily conceived to optimize software and hardware by evolving solutions through a simplified digital model of Darwinian evolution. Subverting the problematic neoliberal notions of survival-of-the-fittest baked into much evolutionary computing, we instead focused on co-adaption, open-ended exploration, and sonic diversity. Queer and feminist notions of kinship were central to this project. They afforded a critique of the norms and biases inherent in evolutionary computing and artificial life. They also allowed for a creative reassessment of these computational methods. Adam's programming work1 was inspired by Stefan Helmreich's ethnography of Artificial Life research at the Santa Fe Institute in the 1990s (2000). Helmreich reads Neo-Darwinist attitudes of his interlocutors against an understanding of kinship that transcends biogenetic relations. The result is an evolving digital-physical ecosystem in which individual sounds enter into non-normative kin-relations (Butler, 2012, 2022) as well as symbiogenetic relationships (Margulis, 2008). Genetic and evolutionary algorithms model biological evolution on a computer, as explained in Adam's work on the topic (Melbye, 2025a). Often, evolutionary algorithms use recombination through crossover as well as mutation on bit-strings or code (representing genomes), to produce new bit-strings or lines of code. If the goal, for example, is to make more efficient code, the algorithm selects the new lines of code that have the smallest size or use less memory and CPU. It then lets them recombine and mutate to produce new generations of increasingly efficient code. Obviously, evolutionary algorithms represent a reductionist model of evolution and lack many of the important processes that characterize “wet” evolution (the kind that include bodily fluids, social interaction, culture and all the other things that make life worth living). Instead of bit-strings, we use sound as the genome at the core of our evolutionary algorithm. These sounds meet other sounds and make kin by exchanging properties. The new sounds then occasionally undergo mutations: some frequencies disappear, or new ones appear. In contrast to many traditional genetic algorithms, the sounds in our implementation also undergo other evolutionary processes, some inspired by biology, some speculative. For example, new sounds may have three parents rather than two, or they may steal genes (frequency information) from the acoustic environment, such as people talking in the exhibition space and cars on the street. The installation (curated by Tuçe Erel) as it was presented at Art Laboratory Berlin in late 2024 included a set of wooden archival boxes with motion sensors, containing catalogue cards and images of artifacts recorded (see Figures 6 and 7). Sounds played through six speakers. A workstation allowed visitors to listen to individual sounds of artifacts and contribute to our open catalogue (see Figure 8), possibly adding information, questions, and thoughts on featured artifacts. A research station with files for each artifact offered additional information. Open 3 days per week for 4 h per day, the recording chosen here is a 2-h edited version of the installation as it sounded on 3 November. During that day, about 12,000 individual impulse responses distributed across approximately 180 generations lived through several life stages to finally reach a ghostly existence from which they could become reborn. This setup cut across different modes of visitor engagement and allowed for a sonic ecology to unfold that sounded different on each day of the installation (see Figure 9). You can watch a short video documenting the installation here: https://vimeo.com/1079346884. A special thank you to Tuçe Erel, Regine Rapp, and Christian de Lutz at Art Laboratory Berlin. Isabel is grateful to have been a fellow of the DAAD program TheMuseumsLab 2024. Finally, we would also like to give thanks to all the beings, powers, and presences that were and are in the vicinity of this sonic ecology, in ways recognized and unrecognized. Open Access funding enabled and organized by Projekt DEAL. All work in ethnographic collections was informed by conversations with curators about the ethical appropriateness of engaging with artifacts. This included considerations of indigenous intellectual property, sacred functions, and cultural belonging statuses of artifacts. We have chosen to engage with artifacts where no conflict of interest could be identified to the best of our own and the curator's knowledge. We are aware that this knowledge may not be comprehensive. The audio file of Queer Sonic Fingerprint includes bits of conversation in different languages. These have been chosen by the algorithm at random from a pool of material. The content of these bits of conversation is not transcribed as many of the original recordings have been filtered. This has changed the overall sound and intelligibility of the content. Conceptually, this is intentional and explained in the ethnographic statement. Code that informed this work, specifically the recording process and the genetic algorithm, is freely available as open-source code on GitHub. Links are integrated in the text. title: Environmental design enhances hearing rehabilitation
abstract: Many public and private listening environments wreak havoc on adults with aging peripheral and central auditory systems. Adults, who may have noted only some difficulty in specific degraded listening environments at an earlier age, may experience extremely frustrating difficulty in these same situations as they age. Older adults may blame this difficulty on the speaker, when in fact the culprits may be the reverberant characteristics of the meeting room, the anechoic environment of their home, or the combined effects of auditory and visual distractions in a multipurpose room within a health care facility. Without recognizing this possibility, older adults may begin to avoid these places and isolate themselves unnecessarily. For audiologists to provide constructive hearing rehabilitation, they must become more than conversant with their patients about the challenges and potential solutions regarding environmental design, which has been shown to provide immediate benefits for patients in many instances. PROBLEM ENVIRONMENTS Meeting rooms, classrooms, church sanctuaries and fellowship halls, nursing home all-purpose rooms, auditoriums, bank lobbies, and many other environments are generally not conducive to hearing and understanding speech. They resemble reverberation chambers (too many almost subliminal echoes), or anechoic environments in which sound does not carry well.FigureThese rooms are often square or rectangular in shape with hard floors (tile, concrete, marble, or wood), sheetrock, concrete block, or brick walls, and they frequently have tile ceilings that are sound-reflective. They usually have white boards or blackboards, uncovered windows, glass-covered pictures, and other sound-reflective surfaces. Most church sanctuaries have hard wooden pews, vaulted ceilings, stained glass windows, hard reflective walls, and hard floors, all sound-reflective or reverberant surfaces. These reflective surfaces cause speech and other sounds to bounce from one surface to another, setting up reverberant echoes that distort sound, particularly complex sounds such as speech. These echoes can play acoustic havoc with impaired peripheral and central auditory systems by distorting the sounds hearing-impaired individuals are attempting to transduce and interpret, particularly if they happen to be wearing hearing aids. In contrast, homes designed for comfort are generally furnished in such a way that they essentially become anechoic chambers. That is, they do not give sound the life that is needed to travel well because there are few, if any, reverberant characteristics that enhance sound transmission. It seems intuitive that too much reverberation, or too many echoes, in a listening environment would be bad for speech understanding and that a typical non-reverberant home environment would enhance hearing, but that is not the case. Many homes designed with comfort in mind restrict the movement of sound by absorbing it before it can travel, which deadens it. Soft carpeting, window drapes, soft chairs and sofas, wall paper, and heavily textured ceilings all absorb sound, and a complex acoustic signal such as speech cannot travel far enough to be heard well from any distance or any angle. Because speech comprises an extremely complex set of acoustic signals, it cannot negotiate stairwells (up or down), travel through doorways, move around corners, or find its way through walls to be received clearly enough by the listener and understood well. Music is a less complex signal, and so will travel with at least a fair degree of accuracy in a home environment—perhaps not the words of the song but the melody at least. In a typical home, speech will not travel well farther than about seven feet in a straight line. If a speaker is farther from the intended listener, it is important that he move within that optimal distance from the listener prior to speaking. This is also a reason to avoid the seats under the balcony in an auditorium or church sanctuary because speech does not travel well in these areas. ENVIRONMENTAL DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS It is not necessary to engage in extensive renovations when working to enhance listening environments. Some environmental modifications can be made by the hearing health care provider. For others, the person with auditory difficulties may have to be his own advocate, and suggest changes that will improve the communicative environment for his specific needs. Audiologists and other care providers can also act as a coach to the patient and his family to assist in making simple environmental changes. A host of ideas are available to help patients by choosing one or two of these strategies that are most appropriate for their individual situation: Meeting rooms, church sanctuaries, and other common places The goal here is to reduce reverberation to enhance the transmission and quality of distortion-free speech so that it is more easily heard and understood. The frustrating aspect of a reverberative listening environment is that the room may actually carry the speech signal so well that the individual may experience little difficulty hearing, or so it seems to the listener. He may think he is hearing fairly well, or at least loudly enough, but may have difficulty understanding what is being said due to crowding of the speech signal. It is important to avoid taking the listening environment from a state in which there is too much reverberation to one that becomes acoustically dead. In other words, the room should not be changed so much that it becomes one without echoes, caused by adding too much absorbency. Because these rooms are typically square or rectangular, patients should do whatever is necessary to alter this shape. This can be done by adding light ceiling-to-floor drapes on an expandable curtain rod to one or two corners of the room, creating a rounder shape and reducing reverberation. Hang light drapes to the sides of windows (not over the windows), with the length two to three inches above and about six to eight inches below the window. If there are no windows, hang light floor-to-ceiling drapes at a few strategic locations on the walls. If the ceiling is higher than most rooms, hang decorative flagging at regular intervals across the ceiling to reduce echoes. If soda machines, ice makers, or water fountains are nearby, make sure that the sound is muffled or quieted as much as possible. If neither option is possible, have these items moved to another location. If a food preparation area is attached to or near the meeting room, use heavy drapes to block off that area to quiet the noise of pots and pans and people talking. Adding a wall with a sliding door to block off the area is an even better solution. Make sure that the PA system is adequate. A poor or unused PA system can be one of the greatest distracters to successful meetings, particularly when there is a speaker for the event. When adding to or installing a new PA system, make sure the speakers are as close to the ceiling as possible with polarity reversed. Acoustic feedback will be avoided, and sound will carry more efficiently because it will drop down over the audience. If PA speakers are at floor level, sound cannot easily rise, and it will be blocked by those sitting in the first row. Coach speakers on how to speak with clarity. This can be done very simply by telling them to slow their rate of speech. Persons over 60 can understand speech best when it is uttered at a rate of around 124 words per minute. The average person speaks at a rate of around 160-180 words per minute, a speed that the human central auditory nervous system is simply not designed to process and comprehend. Instruct speakers how to properly use the microphone. Most microphones in these environments are high impedance, meaning that they resist the voice signal. They are traditionally placed in areas where other extraneous sounds may possibly be picked up, such as a singer in a nightclub with an amplified backup band. These microphones are designed to be held within three to four inches of the mouth. If the amplifier is turned up to compensate for a microphone held farther away, acoustic feedback such as a squealing or whistling will be emitted, and can be quite disturbing to listeners. The amplifier and speakers must be far enough away from the microphone to prevent this from occurring. Advise those responsible for banquets or other activities to avoid background music, or Muzak. No matter how it will set the mood for the event, it competes with speech recognition, and at the least interferes with speech understanding. Homes The home acoustic environment may explain why people generally congregate in the kitchen during family gatherings. Conversations can take place with greater ease because kitchens frequently have a harder floor than other areas of the house, and other hard surfaces such as kitchen tables, cupboards, shelves, and stoves further enhance sound transmission. People generally entertain in the living or family room, but these rooms are typically not ideal environments for conversation, particularly if they contain soft, overstuffed furniture, carpeting, heavy drapes, or textured wallpaper or ceilings. While most people cannot ask homeowners to remove the texture and softness of the living environment, some minor changes can be made to enhance the transmission of the speech sounds—replacing heavy carpeting in a room with laminated wood (throw rugs can still be added to keep a feeling of warmth in the room), substituting heavy drapes with window blinds, or exchanging couches and overstuffed chairs with ones that have greater firmness. These changes should not be instituted simultaneously or in the same room, or the environment may become too reverberant. Auditory distractions must be reduced. Turn the TV or radio volume down or completely off. Do not attempt to communicate with a person who is located around the corner in another room, upstairs, downstairs, or on the other side of an open doorway. The sounds of speech cannot travel well through or around any of these obstacles. To ensure that the person with whom communication is taking place can hear and understand what is being said, advise others not to speak unless the other person can see the face of the speaker—again, not from another room or while walking away from the listener. FigureLighting Careful attention must be paid to lighting when altering the environment. With aging, the color of the eye lens changes, and the speed of dilation or contraction of the iris begins to slow. The lens of the eye also takes on a more opaque coloration, so glare and movement from a brighter environment to one with less light or from less light to a brightly lit environment can be problematic because it becomes more difficult for older adults to use their eyes to communicate. Advise patients to avoid exposed lighting fixtures, uncovered windows, and fluorescent light fixtures. The flicker of fluorescent light can cause tearing of the aging eye, inattentiveness, headaches, and even seizures in those who have never experienced them. Incandescent lighting should be used whenever possible. Other types of lighting can cause problems as well. Mood lighting, candlelight, wall lights, spot lights, and corner illumination in homes, businesses, medical offices, and other locations where older adults are expected to communicate should be avoided. These tend to distort the visual environment for these individuals. Floors covered with no-wax floor polish, polished tile, and highly polished hardwood should also be avoided. Polished linoleum can resemble an ice skating rink to aging eyes, resulting in visual distractions and even possible falls. THE COLLECTIVE GOAL Older adults with impaired hearing and aging visual systems do not, of course, want to appear demented or impaired more than they truly are, but the design of many environments can result in what may be relatively minor impairments becoming unnecessarily amplified. We must provide supportive architecture and practical solutions that will prevent unnecessary impairments of hearing and speech understanding, vision, mobility, and social and mental competence. ENVIRONMENTAL DESIGNFigureRead more on this topic in Dr. Hull's editorial, “Environmental design—An expanding role in hearing rehabilitation for older adults.” (J Rehabil Res Dev 2011; 48[5];xvxviii;http://bit.ly/HullEditorial.)

title: MANUFACTURERS NEWS
abstract: Swedish ALD maker comes to America LOS ANGELES—Comfort Audio (www.comfortaudio.us), an international leader in assistive listening devices (ALDs) and systems since 1994, opened an American sales and marketing office in Los Angeles in January. Ragnar Ahgren, CEO of the Swedish-based Comfort Audio, said, “Our success in Europe and other international markets is based on three fundamental design philosophies: uncompromised technology and sound quality, sophisticated style and attractive designs, and affordability, with products priced for different buyers.”Figure: Comfort ContegoComfort Audio develops only assistive technology. Ahgren explained, “By not competing with hearing aid makers, but rather developing products that are either a complement to hearing aids or a substitute for patients not yet ready for hearing aids, we see our products as easy for dispensers to sell and service and a complement to the products they offer today.” One example of the company's vision is Comfort Contego™, a high-definition digital wireless FM system. According to the company, “the HD sound is crisp and clear and the distinctive look and feel of the small units with easy-to-read digital screens make the device something to show off, not try to hide.” Contego has built-in microphones that are adjustable for maximum customization of sound with omnidirectional or directional sound. The volume for the transmitter can be remotely adjusted from the receiver. In an industry innovation, Contego sends its signals encrypted to prevent electronic eavesdropping. Comfort Duett™, a small, affordable personal amplifier, looks more like an MP3 player than a medical device. Offering up to 60 dB of amplification, it can be integrated into home audio equipment such as TV, music, and a standard telephone. Ahgren says Comfort has big plans in this country. “We didn't come to the US to be an also-ran.” The company says the key to its success is its focus on lifestyle and consumer orientation. While hearing aid users tend to be old people, Comfort Audio says, “Our customers—not patients—are young people—and the young at heart. Our products can easily be mistaken for MP3 players or cool cell phones. Like Apple, whose designs we greatly admire, we make every effort to make our visual and tactile design desirable, something to show off. The audiologist who recognizes the value of offering an affordable and attractive solution for someone not yet ready for hearing aids will establish a bond with a future hearing aid customer.” Phonak's CORE powers new accessories WARRENVILLE, IL—Phonak's (www.phonak.com) new chip technology powers three new digital wireless accessories: iCom brings Bluetooth to the hearing impaired; the myPilot command center provides full-color display feedback; and iCube permits CableFree Fitting. The CORE (communication optimized real-audio engine) technology developed for the chip used in the new Exélia and Naída hearing instruments permits wireless communication between the left and right hearing instruments. Now it has produced a trio of accessory devices.Figure. myPilotiCom is a communication interface that hangs around the neck and fits into the wearer's life like an MP3 player or cell phone. Featuring full stereo sound, broadband audio streaming, FM connectivity, and Bluetooth, it provides unlimited wireless connection to entertainment and communication devices. iCom receives Bluetooth signals from a mobile phone, wirelessly streaming them to Exélia or Naída instruments like a Bluetooth headset. As a result, hearing-impaired people using cell phones will understand better in noisy situations than those with normal hearing. With myPilot, Phonak introduces a generation of remote controls with functionalities that provide access to new features such as ZoomControl. Bi-directional communication between myPilot and the hearing aid allows wearers to change individual settings and obtain useful status information such as battery levels, volume, or current program. Finally, new wireless CORE technology simplifies the programming process for the fitter. Until now, connections between hearing instruments and the PC have been established with cables. The iCube fitting device facilitates CableFree Fitting by streaming the fitting data wirelessly to the hearing instruments. Circle 194 on Reader Service Card A new look, fee, and motto Along with the new accessory devices described above and the Exélia and Naída families of hearing aids and the Inspiro FM system (all reported on in the January Manufacturers News), Phonak un-veiled a new corporate identity and design last month.FigurePhonak's new look and feel are accompanied by a positive statement, “Life is on,” which is also incorporated in this new logo consisting of two adjoining squares. “Life is on” expresses Phonak's quest to roll back the boundaries of technology to develop innovations that help people hear, understand, and experience more of life's rich soundscapes. Initially, the new corporate identity and corporate design will be visible only in conjunction with three products due for imminent rollout, Exélia, Naída, and Inspiro. But further corporate identity and design cornerstones will be developed and implemented over the next few months. Circle 195 on Reader Service Card Hear the World honored BERLIN—Hear the World, a magazine that is part of Phonak's global initiative of the same name to raise awareness of the importance of hearing, was awarded a European Excellence Award 2007 in December. This was its third such honor in 2007, following the Best of Corporate Publishing Award and the iF communication design award.FigureThe magazine won honors in the External Publication category at the ceremony held in Berlin. The European Excellence Award is among the most important prizes in the public relations and communications industry. According to the panel's statement, the magazine uses eye-catching glossy cover designs and extraordinary background reports to create a cultural lifestyle platform that sets itself apart from other corporate publications. The magazine (which is published in English and German) is available at selected newsagents and airports as well as on the Hear the World web site (www.hear-the-world.com). The Hear the World initiative is supported by many world-renowned musicians, including Plácido Domingo, Bryan Adams, the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra, Harry Belafonte, and Moby. Through the Hear the World Foundation, Phonak supports charitable organizations and projects focused on helping people with hearing loss. Circle 196 on Reader Service Card “Virtual patient” for training BALZERS, LIECHTENSTEIN—Otis, the virtual patient (www.audiometry.biz), is a new software program that simulates complex hearing defects so audiometry can be practiced without burdening real patients. Developed largely by Christoph Wille, the software simulates the patient's behavior and quickly detects possible user errors. It guides the learner through exercises at several levels of difficulty and provides feedback.FigureAccording to Wille, Otis shortens the time needed for training, as it can simulate any type of hearing impairment. Thus, students can better develop proficiency in procedures, and then put their new skills into practice sooner. The program also enables experienced practitioners to practice working with complex hearing impairments so they can treat real patients better and more safely. The integration of autonomous learning concepts allows learners to work simply and efficiently, making the best use of their time. Wille de-veloped the training tool in response to a suggestion by a professor at University Hospital in Zurich. Noting a shortage of patients for his training course for audiometrists, the faculty member proposed a simulated computer-based audiometer that would allow trainees to carry out audiometric tests on virtual patients. Wille, a recent graduate of an engineering program, and another young engineer, came up with software that was successfully adopted for audiometry training courses. Otis has been translated into English and other languages and is used in more than 20 countries. Circle 197 on Reader Service Card New leader for Unitron South Africa KITCHENER, ONTARIO—Unitron Hearing (www.unitronhearing.com) has appointed Leonard Marshall as general manager of Unitron Hearing South Africa. He succeeds Debbie Salter. Marshall has 15 years' experience in medical industry sales and product management, primarily for the South African market. Most recent- ly, as national sales manager for a well-known medical com- pany, he oversaw all sales and marketing functions, financial planning, and ex-port business in sub-Saharan Africa.Figure: Leonard MarshallCircle 198 on Reader Service Card Site on hearing protection SMITHFIELD, RI—Howard Leight has launched a hearing protection-oriented web site (www.howardleight.com) that offers visitors a 360° experience in fit, selection, protection, and motivation. It contains a variety of content, including product information, best practices in hearing conservation, and the industry's first hearing protector selector. The hearing protector selector helps people solve their needs by providing a range of solutions for their specific applications. Users can identify their noise exposure levels or specific ratings, product styles, and/or features, and the most applicable results are recommended. These listings can be printed or instantly e-mailed to other people directly from the selector. Users can also learn about a various environmental considerations and preferences or basics of selecting HPDs. Circle 199 on Reader Service Card Soundbridge gets clinical trial for conductive loss DURHAM, NC—Med-El Corporation (www.medel.com) has reported the first U.S. implantation in the clinical trial of the Vibrant Soundbridge® (VSB) as a treatment for conductive and mixed hearing loss using direct round window cochlear stimulation. The Vibrant Soundbridge is the first implantable middle ear hearing device approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat sensorineural hearing loss. Adults with conductive or mixed hearing loss who have been unsuccessful with traditional amplification may be candidates for the trial. The initial implantation was performed in January by Jennifer Maw, MD, founder of Ear and Rehabilitative Services, Inc., in San Jose, CA. She said, “This procedure has the potential to revolutionize how ear surgeons treat chronic ear disease and hearing loss. Eustachian tube dysfunction limits the hearing results that patients can achieve with reconstructive ear surgery, and there are no well-established treatments for this problem. As this device can mimic the function of the middle ear, we can potentially help a large category of patients who could not be previously considered as suitable surgical candidates.” Circle 192 on Reader Service Card Circle 140 on Reader Service Card

title: A Neurocognitive Perspective on Language Acquisition in Ullman’s DP Model
abstract: In the last few decades, the studies in second language acquisition have not answered the question what mechanisms a human’s brain uses to make acquisition of language(s) possible. A neurocognitive model which tries to address SLA from such a perspective was suggested by Ullman (2005; 2015), according to which, “both first and second languages are acquired and processed by well-studied brain systems that are known to subserve particular nonlanguage functions” (Ullman, 2005: 141). The brain systems in question have analogous roles in their language and nonlanguage functions. This article is meant to critically analyse the suggested DP model within the context of neurocognitive studies of L2; and evaluate its contribution to the field of SLA studies.
